Swearing is its own category and can express solidarity, not only offence

points.title: Social distance and rapport
points.detail: The conceptual space between individuals or groups constructed by class, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, education, status and occupation — and rapport as agreement or sympathy between them.

questions.q: Explain what constructs social distance between participants, and describe two linguistic choices a speaker might make to reduce it.
answer: Social distance is constructed by class, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, education, status and occupation.
Choice: shifting to colloquial lexis, slang or hypocoristics to signal shared identity.
Choice: positive politeness — first names, inclusive 'we', agreement, in-group markers.
Reducing distance builds rapport; widening it asserts authority.

card.title: Social distance and rapport
card.front: What constructs social distance, and what is rapport?
back: Social distance — the conceptual space between participants
Built by class, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, education, status, occupation
Greater distance → more formality, more negative politeness
Rapport — agreement, sympathy and ease between participants
Speakers actively reduce distance to build rapport, or widen it to assert authority

points.title: Multi-word lexemes and context-specific graphemes
points.detail: Sequences stored and retrieved as one unit, such as idioms and phrasal verbs; and written symbols whose meaning depends entirely on context.

questions.q: Define a multi-word lexeme and give two examples of different types.
answer: A sequence of words stored and retrieved as a single unit of meaning.
Idiom: 'kick the bucket' — meaning is not derivable from the individual words.
Phrasal verb: 'put up with'.
Also acceptable: compound nouns, fixed collocations.

card.title: Emojis, graphemes and multi-word lexemes
card.front: How do written informal texts replace prosody, and what is a multi-word lexeme?
back: Emojis and emoticons substitute for facial expression and tone
Meaning is context-specific and shifts between groups and generations
Capitals, repeated letters and punctuation stand in for volume and pitch
Context-specific graphemes — symbols meaningful only in their setting
Multi-word lexeme — stored and retrieved as one unit (idioms, phrasal verbs)

papers: 2024 and 2025 English Language examinations. Section A is short-answer on a transcript or text, Section B analytical commentary, Section C an essay.

name: General Mathematics
areas: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology

points.title: Types of data
points.detail: Categorical (nominal or ordinal) and numerical (discrete or continuous). Getting this wrong at the start pushes you into the wrong display and the wrong statistics.

questions.q: Classify each variable: shirt size (S, M, L); number of siblings; time to complete a puzzle; eye colour.
answer: Shirt size — categorical, ordinal (the categories have a natural order).
Number of siblings — numerical, discrete (countable).
Time to complete a puzzle — numerical, continuous.
Eye colour — categorical, nominal (no natural order).

points.title: Displaying categorical data
points.detail: Frequency tables, bar charts and percentaged segmented bar charts, and the mode as the measure of centre.

questions.q: Explain when a percentage segmented bar chart is more useful than a bar chart of counts, and state what its total always represents.
answer: Percentaged charts allow groups of different sizes to be compared fairly.
Raw counts mislead when one group is much larger than another.
Each segmented bar totals 100%.
Percentages must be calculated within each category of the explanatory variable.

points.title: Displaying numerical data
points.detail: Histograms, stem plots and dot plots, and choosing between them according to sample size, context and purpose.

questions.q: A data set of 60 values has a strongly right-skewed distribution with two very large values. State which graphical display is most appropriate and justify your choice.
answer: A histogram or a boxplot — both handle a moderate-to-large data set and show shape clearly.
A boxplot is preferable if the outliers need to be identified individually.
A dot plot or stem plot becomes unwieldy at 60 values and spreads badly with extreme values.
questions.source: 2026 NHT General Exam 1, Q4 — a histogram with a logarithmic scale.

points.title: Describing a distribution
points.detail: Shape (symmetric, positively or negatively skewed), centre, spread and outliers — reported together, in the context of the data.

questions.q: A histogram shows a long tail extending to the right, a peak at the left, and two isolated bars well beyond the tail. Describe the distribution and state which measures of centre and spread should be reported.
answer: Shape: positively (right) skewed, with possible outliers.
Centre should be reported as the median — the mean is dragged upward by the tail and outliers.
Spread should be reported as the IQR for the same reason.
A full description names shape, centre, spread and outliers, with values and units.

points.title: Summary statistics
points.detail: Median, range and IQR for skewed data or data with outliers; mean and standard deviation for approximately symmetric data. Be able to justify the choice.

questions.q: For the data 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 40, calculate the median and explain why it is a better measure of centre than the mean here.
answer: Ordered already; n = 7, so the median is the 4th value = 9.
The mean is 94/7 = 13.4, which is larger than all but two of the values.
40 is an outlier that drags the mean upward.
The median is resistant to outliers, so it better represents a typical value.

points.title: Five-number summary and boxplots
points.detail: The boxplot as the graphical form of the five-number summary, with the lower fence Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and upper fence Q3 + 1.5 × IQR used to identify possible outliers.

questions.q: A data set has Q1 = 24, median = 31, Q3 = 40. Calculate the upper and lower fences and determine whether a value of 66 is an outlier.
answer: 66 > 64, so it is an outlier and is plotted as a separate point on the boxplot.

points.title: The normal distribution and the 68–95–99.7% rule
points.detail: Applying the rule to bell-shaped distributions to find the percentage of values within one, two or three standard deviations of the mean.

questions.q: The weights of a product are normally distributed with mean 500 g and standard deviation 12 g. Find the percentage of products weighing between 476 g and 512 g.
answer: 476 g is 2 standard deviations below the mean; 512 g is 1 above.
From the 68–95–99.7 rule: 95%/2 = 47.5% lies between −2 sd and the mean; 68%/2 = 34% between the mean and +1 sd.
questions.source: 2024 NHT General Exam 1, Q6 — normally distributed can weights.

points.title: Standardised (z) scores
points.detail: Calculating and interpreting them, and using them to compare values that come from different distributions.

questions.q: Test scores are normally distributed with mean 68 and standard deviation 9. A student scores 86. Calculate their standardised score and state the percentage of students who scored below them.
answer: The score is 2 standard deviations above the mean.
From the 68–95–99.7 rule, 95% lie within 2 sd, so 2.5% lie above +2 sd.
97.5% of students scored below them.

points.title: Comparing distributions across groups
points.detail: Parallel boxplots and back-to-back stem plots, comparing centre, spread and outliers, and reporting the differences in context.

questions.q: Two parallel boxplots show group A with median 42 and IQR 10, group B with median 35 and IQR 22. Write a comparison of the two distributions.
answer: Centre: group A has the higher median (42 versus 35), so A's typical value is higher.
Spread: group B is far more variable (IQR 22 versus 10), so B's values are less consistent.
A complete comparison addresses centre, spread, shape and outliers.
Always quote the actual values rather than saying only 'higher' or 'more spread out'.

points.title: Response and explanatory variables
points.detail: Identifying which is which before doing anything else — every later step, including which axis is which, depends on it.

questions.q: A researcher investigates whether hours of study predicts exam score. Identify the response and explanatory variables and explain how you decided.
answer: Explanatory variable: hours of study — the variable used to explain or predict.
Response variable: exam score — the variable being predicted.
The explanatory variable goes on the horizontal axis of a scatterplot.
Getting this the wrong way round invalidates the regression line that follows.

points.title: Two categorical variables
points.detail: Two-way frequency tables and percentaged segmented bar charts, and describing the association by comparing percentages between groups.

questions.q: A two-way table shows that 60 of 150 males and 30 of 100 females prefer option A. Calculate the relevant percentages and state whether an association is present.
answer: Percentages must be calculated within each category of the explanatory variable.
40% versus 30% suggests an association — preference for option A differs by gender.
Always quote both percentages when justifying an association.
questions.source: 2026 NHT General Exam 1, Q5 — opinions about cats and dogs by gender.

points.title: A numerical variable across categories
points.detail: Using parallel boxplots to investigate the association, and describing the difference in medians in context.

questions.q: Explain how parallel boxplots are used to investigate an association between a numerical and a categorical variable, and what would indicate no association.
answer: A separate boxplot is drawn for the numerical variable within each category.
An association is indicated when the medians differ noticeably between categories.
No association when the boxplots have similar medians and similar spreads.
Report the medians with values when justifying your conclusion.

points.title: Scatterplots
points.detail: Describing the association between two numerical variables by direction, form and strength.

questions.q: Describe the three features required when describing the association shown in a scatterplot, and write a full description for a plot showing points falling closely along a downward line.
answer: Direction, form and strength.
Direction: negative. Form: linear. Strength: strong.
Full description: there is a strong, negative, linear association between the two variables.
Name the variables in the description rather than saying 'x and y'.

points.title: Pearson's correlation coefficient r
points.detail: Calculating and interpreting it, and the assumptions it depends on — numerical data, a linear form and no clear outliers.

questions.q: State the three assumptions required for Pearson's correlation coefficient to be an appropriate measure, and interpret a value of r = −0.85.
answer: Both variables are numerical; the association is linear; there are no clear outliers.
r = −0.85 indicates a strong negative linear association.
The sign gives direction; the magnitude gives strength.
r says nothing about causation, and is misleading if the form is non-linear.

points.title: The coefficient of determination
points.detail: r² calculated from r, and interpreted as the percentage of variation in the response variable explained by the explanatory variable — using that exact framing.

questions.q: A regression of exam score on study hours gives r = 0.70. Calculate the coefficient of determination and interpret it in context.
answer: Interpretation: 49% of the variation in exam score can be explained by the variation in study hours.
Use that exact framing — 'explained by the variation in' — or marks are lost.
The remaining 51% is due to other factors.

points.title: Correlation and causation
points.detail: Non-causal explanations for an observed association: coincidence, confounding variables and common response.

questions.q: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents are strongly positively correlated. Explain why this does not show that ice cream causes drownings, naming the relevant non-causal explanation.
answer: Correlation does not establish causation.
This is a common response: a third variable — temperature — influences both.
Hot weather increases both ice cream sales and swimming, and so drowning risk.
Other non-causal explanations are coincidence and confounding variables.

points.title: The least squares line
points.detail: Fitting the line, what 'least squares' actually minimises, and the assumptions behind the method.

questions.q: Explain what the least squares line minimises, and state the assumption that must hold for it to be appropriate.
answer: It minimises the sum of the squared vertical distances (residuals) from each point to the line.
Squaring means positive and negative residuals do not cancel, and large errors are penalised more.
The assumption is that the association is linear.
This is checked with a residual plot — random scatter supports it, a pattern does not.

points.title: Interpreting and using the regression line
points.detail: Interpreting the slope and intercept in the context of the data, making predictions, and the distinction between interpolation and extrapolation.

questions.q: A least squares line is height = 120 + 0.8 × age, fitted for ages 5 to 12. Interpret the slope in context, and explain why predicting the height of a 30-year-old is unsound.
answer: Slope: on average, height increases by 0.8 cm for each additional year of age.
The intercept (120 cm at age 0) has no sensible meaning here — it lies outside the data range.
Predicting at age 30 is extrapolation, well beyond the fitted range of 5 to 12.
The linear relationship cannot be assumed to continue, so the prediction is unreliable.

points.title: Residuals and residual plots
points.detail: Calculating a residual, and using a residual plot to decide whether the linearity assumption holds — a clear pattern means it doesn't.

questions.q: A residual plot shows a clear curved pattern. State what this indicates and what the analyst should do next.
answer: The linear model is not appropriate — the linearity assumption has been violated.
A random scatter about zero would indicate the assumption holds.
Apply a transformation (squared, log or reciprocal) to linearise, then refit the least squares line.

points.title: Data transformation
points.detail: Squared, logarithmic and reciprocal transformations applied to x or y to linearise an association, then fitting and using the transformed model.

questions.q: A scatterplot of y against x is curved, opening upward. A squared transformation is applied to x, giving the line y = 3 + 0.5x². Predict y when x = 4, and explain why the transformation was applied.
answer: Substitute x = 4: x² = 16, so y = 3 + 0.5(16) = 11.
The transformation straightens the relationship so a least squares line can validly be fitted.
Transform the variable on the side that will straighten the curve — check the residual plot afterwards.
questions.source: 2024 NHT General Exam 1, Q11 — a squared transformation to linearise; 2026 NHT Exam 1, Q12 uses a reciprocal.

points.title: Time series plots
points.detail: Describing a time series by trend, seasonality, cycles, structural change, possible outliers and irregular fluctuations.

questions.q: Name four features that should be identified when describing a time series plot, and state what distinguishes a cycle from seasonality.
answer: Trend, seasonality, cycles, irregular fluctuations — plus outliers and structural change.
Seasonality repeats over a fixed and known period, such as quarters or months.
A cycle repeats over a longer and variable period with no fixed length.
Structural change is an abrupt, lasting shift in the pattern.

points.title: Smoothing
points.detail: Moving means with an odd number of points, moving means with an even number and centring, and moving medians — including smoothing graphically.

questions.q: The daily values are 14, 18, 11, 20, 16, 22, 19. Calculate the three-median smoothed value for the fourth day.
answer: Three-median smoothing uses the value and its immediate neighbours.
For day 4: the values are 11, 20, 16.
Ordered: 11, 16, 20 — the median is 16.
Smoothed value for day 4 is 16.
questions.source: 2026 NHT General Exam 1, Q13 — a five-median smoothed value for a share price.

points.title: Seasonal indices
points.detail: Calculating them, interpreting what an index above or below 1 means, and deseasonalising and reseasonalising data.

questions.q: Quarterly sales for quarter 3 are $48 000 and the seasonal index for quarter 3 is 1.2. Calculate the deseasonalised figure, and state what the index value tells you.
answer: Deseasonalised = actual / seasonal index = 48 000 / 1.2 = $40 000.
An index above 1 means quarter 3 sales are typically higher than average.
Specifically, 20% above the quarterly average.
The four quarterly indices must sum to 4.
questions.source: 2026 NHT General Exam 1, Q15 and Q16 — deseasonalised sales and a missing seasonal index.

points.title: Forecasting
points.detail: Fitting a least squares line to deseasonalised time series data, forecasting forward, and reseasonalising the forecast.

questions.q: A least squares line fitted to deseasonalised quarterly sales is sales = 2400 + 150 × quarter number. The seasonal index for quarter 4 is 1.3. Forecast the actual sales for quarter 12.
answer: Deseasonalised forecast: 2400 + 150 × 12 = 2400 + 1800 = 4200.
Quarter 12 is a fourth quarter, so reseasonalise using the index 1.3.
Actual forecast = 4200 × 1.3 = 5460.
Deseasonalise by dividing; reseasonalise by multiplying.

points.title: First-order linear recurrence relations
points.detail: Reading a relation of the form u₀ = a, uₙ₊₁ = Ruₙ + d, generating terms, and deducing the explicit rule.

questions.q: A recurrence relation is V₀ = 5000, V_(n+1) = 0.85V_n + 200. Calculate V₁ and V₂, and state what the two constants represent.
answer: 0.85 is the multiplier — here a 15% reduction each period.
200 is a fixed amount added each period, independent of the balance.

points.title: Flat rate depreciation
points.detail: The recurrence relation and the rule for the value after n periods, and the straight-line graph it produces.

questions.q: A machine costing $24 000 is depreciated by the flat rate method at 12% per annum. Write the recurrence relation and find its value after 4 years.
answer: Flat rate depreciates by 12% of the ORIGINAL value each year: 0.12 × 24 000 = $2880.
The graph is a straight line — constant reduction each period.

points.title: Unit cost depreciation
points.detail: Depreciation by use rather than time, and setting up the relation when the rate is per kilometre or per item.

questions.q: A van bought for $45 000 depreciates at 18 cents per kilometre. Find its value after travelling 60 000 km, and state one advantage of unit cost over flat rate depreciation.
answer: Unit cost reflects actual use rather than elapsed time.
A vehicle driven little retains more value, which matches reality better than a time-based method.

points.title: Reducing balance depreciation
points.detail: The recurrence relation and rule, and why the value never quite reaches zero.

questions.q: Equipment worth $18 000 depreciates by the reducing balance method at 20% per annum. Find its value after 3 years, and explain why it never reaches zero.
answer: Each year the value is multiplied by 0.80: V_(n+1) = 0.80V_n.
Each year removes 20% of the CURRENT value, which shrinks each time.
The amount removed keeps decreasing, so the value approaches but never reaches zero.

points.title: Simple interest
points.detail: Investments and loans modelled with linear growth, and the link to flat rate depreciation as the same mathematics.

questions.q: $7500 is invested at 5.2% per annum simple interest. Calculate the interest earned in 3 years and the final balance, and state how simple interest relates to flat rate depreciation.
answer: Annual interest = 0.052 × 7500 = $390.
Both are linear — a fixed amount is added or removed each period, based on the original value.

points.title: Compound interest
points.detail: The recurrence relation and rule, converting between annual and per-period rates, and the effective annual interest rate.

questions.q: An investment of $6000 earns 4.8% per annum compounding monthly. Write the recurrence relation and find the balance after 2 years.
answer: Monthly rate = 4.8/12 = 0.4%, so R = 1.004.

points.title: Reducing balance loans
points.detail: Amortisation tables, and splitting each repayment into its interest and principal reduction components.

questions.q: A $20 000 reducing balance loan at 6% per annum compounding monthly is repaid with monthly payments of $400. Calculate the interest charged in the first month and the balance after the first payment.
answer: Monthly rate = 6/12 = 0.5%.
Principal reduction = 400 − 100 = $300.
Balance after first payment = 20 000 − 300 = $19 700.

points.title: Using a finance solver
points.detail: Entering the five quantities correctly, getting the signs right, and solving for the payment, the number of periods, the rate or the balance.

questions.q: Using a finance solver for a loan, state what each of N, I%, PV, PMT and FV represents, and explain the sign convention.
answer: N = number of payment periods; I% = annual interest rate; PV = present value (amount borrowed).
PMT = payment per period; FV = future value (balance remaining).
Money received is positive and money paid out is negative, so for a loan PV is positive and PMT negative.
Getting the signs wrong is the single most common source of error.

points.title: Interest-only loans
points.detail: The condition that makes a loan interest-only, and the repayment required to hold the balance constant.

questions.q: A $150 000 interest-only loan is charged 5.4% per annum compounding monthly. Calculate the required monthly repayment and explain why the balance never reduces.
answer: Monthly rate = 5.4/12 = 0.45%.
Interest per month = 150 000 × 0.0045 = $675.
Repayment must equal the interest charged, so $675 per month.
Because the payment exactly cancels the interest, no principal is repaid and the balance stays at $150 000.

points.title: Annuities
points.detail: Drawing down an investment with regular withdrawals, the recurrence relation, and the amortisation table.

questions.q: A retiree invests $400 000 at 4.2% per annum compounding monthly and withdraws $2500 each month. Calculate the balance after one month and explain whether this annuity will eventually be exhausted.
answer: The withdrawal exceeds the interest, so the balance falls each month.
It will eventually be exhausted — this is an annuity, not a perpetuity.

points.title: Perpetuities
points.detail: The condition for a payment to continue indefinitely, and calculating the payment or the principal required.

questions.q: A $250 000 fund earns 5.4% per annum compounding monthly. Determine the maximum monthly payment that can be made in perpetuity.
answer: A perpetuity requires the payment to exactly equal the interest earned each period.
Monthly rate = 5.4/12 = 0.45%.
Payment = 250 000 × 0.0045 = $1125 per month.
Any larger payment erodes the principal and the fund eventually runs out.

points.title: Annuity investments
points.detail: Compound interest investments with regular equal additions to the principal, and the rule for the balance after n periods.

questions.q: An annuity investment starts at $5000 with $200 added at the end of each month, earning 3.6% per annum compounding monthly. Write the recurrence relation and find the balance after two months.

points.title: Changing conditions
points.detail: Handling an interest rate change, an extra lump sum or a change in repayment partway through, by restarting the model from the current balance.

questions.q: A $30 000 loan at 6% per annum compounding monthly has repayments of $600. After 12 months the rate rises to 7.2%. Explain how you would find the new balance after a further 6 months.
answer: Run the first 12 months at a monthly rate of 0.5% with PMT = 600, and record the balance.
That balance becomes the new present value — restart the model from it.
Run the next 6 months at the new monthly rate of 7.2/12 = 0.6%.
Never apply an average rate across the whole term; solve each stage separately.

points.title: Matrices, order and types
points.detail: Order as rows × columns, and the row, column, square, zero, identity, diagonal, symmetric and triangular types.

questions.q: Matrix A has 3 rows and 4 columns. State its order, the element a₂₃'s position, and whether A + Aᵀ is defined.
answer: Order is 3 × 4, always rows × columns.
a₂₃ is the element in row 2, column 3.
Aᵀ has order 4 × 3, so A + Aᵀ is not defined.
Addition requires both matrices to have identical order.

points.title: Addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication
points.detail: Including the condition that the matrices must have the same order.

answer: Subtract B element by element.

points.title: Matrix multiplication and powers
points.detail: The condition for the product to be defined, why order matters, and raising a square matrix to a power.

questions.q: Given A of order 2 × 3 and B of order 3 × 2, state whether AB and BA are defined, give the order of each that is, and explain the general rule.
answer: AB is defined: the inner dimensions (3 and 3) match. Order of AB is 2 × 2.
BA is also defined: inner dimensions (2 and 2) match. Order of BA is 3 × 3.
Rule: (m × n)(n × p) is defined and gives an m × p matrix.
AB and BA are generally different — matrix multiplication is not commutative.

points.title: Matrices in practical problems
points.detail: Storing and manipulating information — costing and pricing, inventories, and using row or column summing matrices to total rows or columns.

questions.q: A 1×3 matrix of prices [4 6 9] and a 3×1 column matrix of quantities [10; 5; 2] are multiplied. State the order of the product, calculate it, and explain what it represents.
answer: A 1×3 multiplied by a 3×1 gives a 1×1 matrix.
The product represents the total cost of the items.

points.title: Determinant and inverse
points.detail: The determinant of a 2 × 2 matrix, finding the inverse, and recognising a singular matrix with no inverse.

questions.q: For A = [[4, 2], [3, 1]], calculate the determinant and the inverse.
answer: For [[a, b], [c, d]] the inverse is (1/det)[[d, −b], [−c, a]].
= [[−0.5, 1], [1.5, −2]]. If det were 0 the matrix would be singular with no inverse.

points.title: Solving simultaneous equations with matrices
points.detail: Writing a system in matrix form and solving it using the inverse.

questions.q: Solve the system 2x + 3y = 13 and x − y = 1 using matrix methods.
answer: det A = (2)(−1) − (3)(1) = −5, so the inverse exists.

points.title: Communication and dominance matrices
points.detail: Squaring a matrix to count two-step links, and combining matrices to rank individuals by dominance.

questions.q: In a dominance matrix for four teams, explain what squaring the matrix achieves and how an overall ranking is produced.
answer: The original matrix records one-step dominances — who directly beat whom.
Squaring it counts two-step dominances: A beat B, and B beat C.
Add the one-step and two-step matrices to give a combined score for each competitor.
Rank by summing each row of that combined matrix, highest total first.

points.title: Permutation matrices
points.detail: Using a matrix to reorder the rows or columns of another matrix, and the effect of applying it repeatedly.

questions.q: Explain what a permutation matrix does, and state what happens when one is applied repeatedly to the same column matrix.
answer: A permutation matrix reorders the rows (or columns) of another matrix.
It contains exactly one 1 in each row and each column, with all other entries 0.
Applying it repeatedly cycles the entries through a repeating pattern.
After a fixed number of applications the original order returns.

points.title: Transition and state matrices
points.detail: Building a transition matrix from a diagram or a worded description, with columns summing to one, and defining the initial state matrix.

questions.q: In a town, 80% of bus users continue next month and 20% switch to driving; 10% of drivers switch to the bus. Write the transition matrix and find the state after one month if 500 use the bus and 900 drive.
answer: T = [[0.8, 0.1], [0.2, 0.9]], with columns summing to 1 and order (bus, drive).

points.title: Long-run behaviour
points.detail: Using Sₙ = Tⁿ S₀ to find a future state, and finding the steady state that the system settles towards.

questions.q: Explain what a steady state solution is for a transition matrix model, and describe how to find it using technology.
answer: The steady state is the distribution that no longer changes from one step to the next.
Compute Sₙ = Tⁿ S₀ for increasingly large n until the values stabilise.
In practice raising T to a high power, such as T⁵⁰, gives columns that are identical.
The steady state does not depend on the initial state matrix for a regular transition matrix.

points.title: Transition matrices with additions
points.detail: Models of the form Sₙ₊₁ = T Sₙ + B, where a fixed number is added or removed each step, and why no steady state may exist.

questions.q: A population is modelled by S_(n+1) = T·S_n + B where B = [50; −20]. Explain what B represents and why this model may have no steady state.
answer: B is a fixed quantity added to or removed from each category every step, independent of the transition proportions.
Here 50 are added to the first category and 20 removed from the second each period.
Because the additions do not depend on the current state, the totals can grow or shrink without limit.
The system may therefore never settle to a steady state, unlike a pure T·S_n model.

points.title: Leslie matrices
points.detail: Population models split into age groups, with birth rates in the first row and survival rates on the subdiagonal.

questions.q: A Leslie matrix has first row [0 1.4 0.8] and subdiagonal entries 0.6 and 0.3. Explain what each set of values represents.
answer: The first row holds birth rates: the average offspring produced by each age group per period.
Age group 1 produces none; group 2 produces 1.4; group 3 produces 0.8.
The subdiagonal holds survival rates: 0.6 of group 1 survive into group 2, and 0.3 of group 2 into group 3.
All other entries are zero — individuals can only advance one age group per period.

points.title: Graph terminology
points.detail: Vertex, edge, loop, multiple edge and degree. Directed and undirected, simple, connected, complete, bipartite graphs and subgraphs.

questions.q: Define degree, and for a graph with 5 vertices of degrees 2, 3, 3, 4 and 4, determine the number of edges.
answer: The degree of a vertex is the number of edge-ends attached to it; a loop contributes 2.
Sum of degrees = 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 4 = 16.
The sum of degrees equals twice the number of edges.

points.title: Adjacency matrices
points.detail: Constructing one from a graph and reading a graph off one, including how loops are counted.

questions.q: Explain how an adjacency matrix records a graph, including how loops are represented, and state why the matrix is symmetric for an undirected graph.
answer: Entry (i, j) gives the number of edges directly connecting vertex i to vertex j.
A loop at vertex i is conventionally recorded as 1 in position (i, i) for an undirected graph.
In an undirected graph an edge from i to j is also an edge from j to i.
So entry (i, j) equals entry (j, i), making the matrix symmetric.

points.title: Planar graphs and Euler's formula
points.detail: Redrawing a graph so no edges cross, and applying v − e + f = 2.

questions.q: A connected planar graph has 7 vertices and 11 edges. Use Euler's formula to find the number of faces.
answer: Euler's formula: v − e + f = 2.
The count of faces includes the infinite outer region.

points.title: Walks, trails, paths, circuits and cycles
points.detail: The distinctions between them, which is where most of the marks in this topic are won or lost.

questions.q: Define a walk, a trail, a path and a cycle, and state what distinguishes each from the one before it.
answer: Walk: any sequence of edges from one vertex to another; repeats allowed.
Trail: a walk with no repeated edge (vertices may repeat).
Path: a walk with no repeated vertex, and therefore no repeated edge.
Cycle: a path that starts and finishes at the same vertex. A circuit is a trail that does the same.

points.title: Eulerian trails and circuits
points.detail: The conditions in terms of the number of odd-degree vertices, and where such a trail must start and finish.

questions.q: A graph has exactly two vertices of odd degree. State whether an Eulerian trail and an Eulerian circuit exist, and where any trail must begin and end.
answer: An Eulerian trail exists — a graph with exactly two odd vertices has one.
No Eulerian circuit exists; that requires every vertex to have even degree.
The trail must start at one odd vertex and finish at the other.
Eulerian routes use every EDGE exactly once.

points.title: Hamiltonian paths and cycles
points.detail: Visiting every vertex once, and the difference from the Eulerian case which visits every edge.

questions.q: Distinguish a Hamiltonian path from a Hamiltonian cycle, and explain how both differ from the Eulerian equivalents.
answer: Hamiltonian path: visits every VERTEX exactly once.
Hamiltonian cycle: does the same and returns to the starting vertex.
Eulerian routes use every EDGE exactly once instead.
There is no simple degree test for the existence of a Hamiltonian route.

points.title: Trees and spanning trees
points.detail: The defining properties of a tree, and identifying a spanning tree within a larger graph.

questions.q: Define a tree and a spanning tree, and state how many edges a spanning tree of a graph with 9 vertices must contain.
answer: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles.
A spanning tree is a subgraph that is a tree and includes every vertex of the original graph.
A tree on n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges.
So a spanning tree here has 8 edges.

points.title: Minimum spanning trees
points.detail: Applying Prim's algorithm and reporting the total weight of the resulting tree.

questions.q: Describe how Prim's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree, and state one reason a minimum spanning tree might not be unique.
answer: Start at any vertex. Add the cheapest edge connecting the tree to a vertex not yet included.
Repeat until every vertex is connected, never adding an edge that would form a cycle.
Stop after n − 1 edges have been added.
If two edges have equal weight at a choice point, different valid trees of the same total weight can result.

points.title: Shortest path problems
points.detail: Solving by inspection for small networks and by Dijkstra's algorithm for larger ones.

questions.q: Explain how Dijkstra's algorithm finds a shortest path, and state one situation where inspection is sufficient instead.
answer: It assigns each vertex a tentative distance from the start, beginning at zero.
It repeatedly selects the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance and updates its neighbours.
The process ends when the destination is reached with a confirmed minimum.
For a small network with few routes, checking each path by inspection is faster and less error-prone.

points.title: Flow problems
points.detail: Capacities, sources and sinks, identifying cuts and their capacity, and using the minimum cut to find the maximum flow.

questions.q: A network has three cuts separating source from sink with capacities 24, 19 and 27. State the maximum flow and explain the reasoning.
answer: The maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut.
The minimum of 24, 19 and 27 is 19.
Maximum flow = 19.
A valid cut must sever every path from source to sink, and only edges directed source-to-sink count toward its capacity.

points.title: Matching problems
points.detail: Bipartite graphs and allocation, and using the Hungarian algorithm to find the optimal assignment.

questions.q: Explain what a bipartite graph is and how the Hungarian algorithm is used in an allocation problem.
answer: A bipartite graph has two distinct sets of vertices, with edges only between the sets, never within one.
In allocation, one set is workers and the other tasks, with edge weights giving cost or time.
The Hungarian algorithm subtracts row and column minimums, then covers zeros with the fewest lines.
It finds the allocation with the lowest total cost, one worker to one task.

points.title: Project networks
points.detail: Building a network from a table of activities, durations and immediate predecessors, including the use of dummy activities.

questions.q: Activities: A (3 days, no predecessor), B (5, no predecessor), C (4, after A), D (2, after A and B), E (6, after C and D). Determine the minimum completion time.
answer: Path A–C–E: 3 + 4 + 6 = 13 days.
Path A–D–E: 3 + 2 + 6 = 11 days.
Path B–D–E: 5 + 2 + 6 = 13 days.
Minimum completion time = 13 days; both A–C–E and B–D–E are critical.

points.title: Forward and backward scanning
points.detail: Earliest start times, latest start times, and calculating the float of each activity.

questions.q: For an activity with earliest start time 7, duration 4, and latest finish time 15, calculate the float and state whether the activity is critical.
answer: Earliest finish time = 7 + 4 = 11.
Latest start time = 15 − 4 = 11.
Float = latest start − earliest start = 11 − 7 = 4 days.
Float is non-zero, so the activity is not on the critical path.

points.title: Critical path analysis
points.detail: Identifying the critical path, the minimum completion time, and which activities have no float.

questions.q: Explain what the critical path represents in a project network, how it is identified, and why a manager would monitor it closely.
answer: It is the longest path through the network, and so sets the minimum project completion time.
Identified by forward and backward scanning — activities with zero float are on it.
Any delay to a critical activity delays the whole project by the same amount.
Non-critical activities have float and can slip without affecting the finish date.

points.title: Crashing
points.detail: Reducing activity durations at a cost, and recognising when the critical path shifts to a different sequence.

questions.q: A project has critical path A–C–E of 13 days and a second path B–D–E of 12 days. Activity C is crashed by 3 days. Determine the new minimum completion time.
answer: Crashing C by 3 reduces A–C–E from 13 to 10 days.
B–D–E is unaffected and remains 12 days.
The critical path has shifted to B–D–E, so the new completion time is 12 days.
Crashing beyond the point where another path becomes critical gains nothing.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Modelling in context
points.detail: Selecting a standard model for a practical situation, and stating the assumptions and conditions it relies on.

questions.q: A student models a population with a recurrence relation assuming a constant growth rate. State two assumptions this model makes and one limitation that follows.
answer: Assumes the growth rate stays constant over every period modelled.
Assumes no external shocks — no migration, disease or resource limit.
Limitation: predictions become unreliable over long time spans as conditions change.
Stating assumptions is part of the modelling process, not an optional extra.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Computational thinking and algorithms
points.detail: Abstraction, decomposition, pattern and algorithm applied to problem-solving, and following an algorithm step by step.

questions.q: An algorithm is: set total to 0; for each value in the list, if the value is above 50, add it to total; report total. State what the algorithm computes and identify the decision and repetition steps.
answer: It computes the sum of all values greater than 50.
Repetition: 'for each value in the list' — the loop.
Decision: 'if the value is above 50' — the conditional.
Sequencing, decision and repetition are the three building blocks of any algorithm.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Exact versus approximate results
points.detail: Knowing which form your technology has given you, and rounding to a stated number of decimal places or significant figures.

questions.q: A finance solver returns a repayment of 486.3271. State how this should be reported for a monthly loan repayment and explain why.
answer: Report as $486.33, rounded UP to the nearest cent.
Money is quoted to two decimal places.
For a repayment that must clear a loan, rounding down would leave a small balance outstanding.
Always check whether the question specifies rounding — if it does, follow it exactly.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Using technology well
points.detail: The finance solver, statistics and regression functions, and matrix operations — choosing the right one and verifying the output rather than trusting it.

questions.q: A student enters PV = −20000 and PMT = −400 into a finance solver for a loan and gets an impossible answer. Explain the error and give the correct sign convention.
answer: Both values have the same sign, which the solver interprets as money flowing the same direction.
Convention: money received is positive, money paid out is negative.
For a loan you receive the principal, so PV = +20000, and you pay the repayments, so PMT = −400.
Always check the answer is plausible before using it.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Interpreting and reporting results
points.detail: Reporting an answer in the context of the problem, with units, and discussing the limitations of the model used.

questions.q: A student reports 'the answer is 13'. Explain what is missing and rewrite it for a project network question about completion time.
answer: No units, no context, and no indication of what the number measures.
Rewritten: 'The minimum completion time for the project is 13 days.'
State the quantity, the value and the unit, in the context of the question.
Where relevant, comment on whether the answer is reasonable.

papers: VCAA 2020–2026 General/Further examinations and NHT papers, plus commercial trial exams, in your General folder. Several have full worked solutions. Exam 1 is 40 multiple-choice; Exam 2 is written response across the four modules.

name: Mathematical Methods
areas: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Graphs of polynomial functions
points.detail: Key features by degree — axis intercepts, turning points, end behaviour. Sketching by hand up to degree 4, and reading a rule off a graph.

questions.q: For f(x) = x³ − 4x, state the x-intercepts, describe the end behaviour, and state the number of turning points.
answer: Factorise: x(x² − 4) = x(x − 2)(x + 2), so intercepts at x = −2, 0, 2.
As x → ∞, f(x) → ∞; as x → −∞, f(x) → −∞ (positive leading coefficient, odd degree).
A cubic with three distinct real roots has two turning points.

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Power functions
points.detail: y = xⁿ for n ∈ Q. Shape for positive, negative and fractional n; maximal domain and range; asymptotic behaviour where it applies.

questions.q: State the maximal domain and the range of f(x) = x^(1/2) − 3, and describe the shape of its graph.
answer: Maximal domain: [0, ∞) — the square root requires a non-negative argument.
Shape: the graph of y = √x translated 3 units down; increasing, concave down, endpoint at (0, −3).

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Exponential functions
points.detail: y = aˣ for a ∈ R, and y = eˣ in particular. The key points (−1, 1/a), (0, 1) and (1, a), the horizontal asymptote, and growth vs decay.

questions.q: The graph of y = 2e^(x−1) + 3 is obtained from y = e^x. State the transformations applied in order, the equation of the horizontal asymptote, and the y-intercept.
answer: Dilation by factor 2 from the x-axis, translation 1 unit right, translation 3 units up.
Horizontal asymptote: y = 3.
y-intercept: x = 0 gives y = 2e^(−1) + 3 = 2/e + 3 ≈ 3.74.

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Logarithmic functions
points.detail: y = logₑ(x) and y = log₁₀(x). Vertical asymptote, domain, and the inverse relationship with the exponential function.

questions.q: For y = log_e(2x − 6), state the maximal domain, the equation of the vertical asymptote, and the x-intercept.
answer: Requires 2x − 6 > 0, so domain is (3, ∞).
Vertical asymptote: x = 3.
x-intercept when 2x − 6 = 1, so x = 3.5.

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Circular functions
points.detail: y = sin(x), y = cos(x) and y = tan(x). Amplitude, period, range, exact values, and the asymptotes of tan.

questions.q: State the amplitude, period and range of y = −3 sin(2x) + 1, and give the coordinates of its first maximum for x ≥ 0.
answer: Amplitude 3; period 2π/2 = π; range [−2, 4].
The negative coefficient reflects the graph, so the first maximum occurs where sin(2x) = −1.
2x = 3π/2, so x = 3π/4, giving the point (3π/4, 4).
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 2, Q1 and Q2 — range and asymptotes of circular functions.

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Transformations
points.detail: y = A f(n(x + b)) + c where A, n ≠ 0. Dilations (both 'parallel to' and 'from' an axis), reflections and translations, and the order in which they apply.

questions.q: Describe the sequence of transformations mapping y = f(x) to y = −f(2(x + 1)) − 4, in the correct order.
answer: Dilation by factor 1/2 from the y-axis (parallel to the x-axis).
Translation 1 unit in the negative x direction.
Reflection in the x-axis, then translation 4 units down.
Dilations and reflections are applied before translations.

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: The inverse transformation
points.detail: Working backwards from a transformed graph to the original function, and describing the mapping that does it.

questions.q: The graph of y = f(x) is transformed to y = 3f(x − 2). Describe the transformation that maps the new graph back to the original.
answer: Reverse each transformation, in reverse order.
Translate 2 units in the negative x direction.
Then dilate by factor 1/3 from the x-axis.
Mapping: (x, y) → (x − 2, y/3).

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Families of transformed functions
points.detail: How the graph changes as a single transformation parameter varies, and what stays fixed.

questions.q: For the family y = x² + bx + 1 where b ∈ R, determine the values of b for which the graph has no x-intercepts.
answer: No x-intercepts when the discriminant is negative.

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Sum and difference functions
points.detail: Graphs of f + g and f − g, including the domain of the result being the intersection of the two domains.

questions.q: Given f(x) = √x with domain [0, ∞) and g(x) = x − 2 with domain R, state the domain of (f + g)(x) and find (f + g)(4).
answer: Domain of a sum is the intersection of the domains: [0, ∞).

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Product functions
points.detail: The graph of f × g, including where it cuts the axes and how the factors' signs determine its shape.

questions.q: For f(x) = x and g(x) = x − 3, sketch the key features of y = f(x)g(x), stating the x-intercepts and the coordinates of the turning point.
answer: The product is x(x − 3) = x² − 3x, a parabola.
x-intercepts at x = 0 and x = 3 — where either factor is zero.
Turning point midway at x = 1.5, giving (1.5, −2.25).

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Composite functions
points.detail: Graphs of f ∘ g. The existence condition ran(g) ⊆ dom(f), and finding the domain and range of the composite. Composites giving reciprocal or quotient functions are excluded.

questions.q: Let f(x) = √x with domain [0, ∞) and g(x) = x − 5 with domain R. Determine whether f(g(x)) is defined, and if so state its rule and domain.
answer: f(g(x)) requires ran(g) ⊆ dom(f). ran(g) = R, dom(f) = [0, ∞), so not defined on all of R.
Restricting: need x − 5 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 5.
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 2, Q10 — an inequality involving a composite function.

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: Modelling practical situations
points.detail: Using polynomial, power, circular, exponential and logarithmic functions, their transformations and combinations, including simple piecewise (hybrid) functions.

questions.q: The depth of water in a harbour is modelled by d(t) = 4 + 2sin(πt/6), where t is hours after midnight. State the maximum depth, the time it first occurs, and the period of the model.
answer: Maximum depth = 4 + 2 = 6 metres, when sin(πt/6) = 1.
πt/6 = π/2 gives t = 3, so 3 am.
Period = 2π ÷ (π/6) = 12 hours.
Minimum depth is 2 metres, at 9 am.

points.area: Area of Study 1 — Functions, relations and graphs
points.title: The language of key features
points.detail: Domain, maximal or implied domain, co-domain, range, asymptotic behaviour, symmetry, stationary points and points of inflection — used precisely, because marks hang on the wording.

questions.q: Explain the difference between the maximal (implied) domain of a function and a restricted domain, using y = 1/(x − 2) as your example.
answer: The maximal domain is every value of x for which the rule is defined: R \ {2}.
A restricted domain is a smaller domain deliberately imposed, e.g. (2, ∞).
Restricting is often done to make a function one-to-one so an inverse exists.

points.area: Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
points.title: Solving polynomial equations
points.detail: Real coefficients, degree n with up to n real solutions. Factor and remainder theorems, the rational root theorem, and numerical solutions where exact ones aren't required.

questions.q: Given that x = 2 is a solution of x³ − 3x² − 4x + 12 = 0, factorise the cubic fully and state all solutions.
answer: Since x = 2 is a root, (x − 2) is a factor.
Dividing: x³ − 3x² − 4x + 12 = (x − 2)(x² − x − 6).
Factorise the quadratic: (x − 3)(x + 2).
Solutions: x = −2, 2, 3.

points.area: Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
points.title: Inverse functions
points.detail: The condition for an inverse to exist (one-to-one, or a restricted domain that makes it so), finding the rule, swapping domain and range, and the reflection in y = x.

questions.q: For f(x) = (x − 1)² with domain [1, ∞), find the rule and domain of f⁻¹, and explain why the domain restriction was necessary.
answer: Let y = (x − 1)², swap: x = (y − 1)², so y = 1 + √x (taking the positive root to match the restricted domain).
f⁻¹(x) = 1 + √x, domain [0, ∞) — which is the range of f.
Without restriction, f is many-to-one, so no inverse function exists.
The domain of the inverse is the range of the original.

points.area: Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
points.title: Using inverses to solve equations
points.detail: Applying inverse operations to exponential, logarithmic, circular and power equations.

questions.q: Solve 3e^(2x) − 5 = 16 for x, giving an exact answer.
answer: Take the natural log of both sides: 2x = log_e(7).
x = ½ log_e(7).

points.area: Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
points.title: Composition of functions
points.detail: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)), defined when ran(g) ⊆ dom(f). Finding the rule, domain and range of a composite.

questions.q: Let f(x) = x² and g(x) = 2x + 1, both with domain R. Find the rules for f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) and state why they differ.
answer: Composition is not commutative — the order in which the operations are applied changes the result.

points.area: Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
points.title: Solving f(x) = g(x)
points.detail: Over a specified interval, by graphical, numerical and algebraic methods, choosing whichever is appropriate.

questions.q: Solve x² − 4 = 3x − 6 algebraically, and state what the solutions represent graphically.
answer: x = 1 and x = 2.
These are the x-coordinates of the points where the parabola y = x² − 4 and the line y = 3x − 6 intersect.

points.area: Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
points.title: Literal equations and equations with a parameter
points.detail: Solving for x in terms of constants, and finding the general solution — including the values of the parameter for which no solution or infinitely many exist.

questions.q: Consider the system kx + 3y = 6 and 2x + ky = 4, where k ∈ R. Find the values of k for which the system has no solution.
answer: Write as a matrix and use the determinant: det = k·k − 3·2 = k² − 6.
A unique solution exists when k² − 6 ≠ 0, i.e. k ≠ ±√6.
When k = √6 the equations are inconsistent (check by substitution) so there is no solution.
Always test both values — one may give infinitely many solutions instead of none.
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 2, Q4 — a system of equations containing a parameter k.

points.area: Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
points.title: Simultaneous linear equations
points.detail: Including the cases of no solution and infinitely many solutions. Geometric interpretation is required for two equations in two variables only.

questions.q: For what value of m do the equations 2x + 3y = 7 and 4x + my = 14 have infinitely many solutions? Explain geometrically.
answer: Infinitely many solutions when one equation is a multiple of the other.
The second is twice the first when m = 6: 4x + 6y = 14.
Geometrically the two lines coincide — they are the same line, so every point on it is a solution.
If m = 6 but the constant were not 14, the lines would be parallel and there would be no solution.

points.area: Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
points.title: Exponent and logarithm laws
points.detail: Applied to simplifying expressions and solving equations, including changing base and dealing with restrictions on the domain.

questions.q: Solve log_e(x) + log_e(x − 3) = log_e(10) for x.
answer: Combine: log_e(x(x − 3)) = log_e(10), so x² − 3x = 10.
x² − 3x − 10 = 0, giving (x − 5)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 5 or x = −2.
Reject x = −2: the domain requires x > 3 for both logarithms to be defined.

points.area: Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
points.title: Exact solutions of trigonometric equations
points.detail: Solving sin(ax + b) = c, cos(ax + b) = c and tan(ax + b) = c by hand over a given interval, finding every solution in that interval rather than just the first.

questions.q: Solve 2 sin(2x) = √3 for x ∈ [0, 2π], giving exact values.
answer: sin(2x) = √3/2. Let u = 2x, where u ∈ [0, 4π].
sin(u) = √3/2 at u = π/3, 2π/3, and then adding 2π: 7π/3, 8π/3.
Change the interval for u first — that is where solutions are usually lost.
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 1, Q3b — solving a circular function equation over an interval.

points.area: Area of Study 2 — Algebra, number and structure
points.title: Newton's method
points.detail: The algorithm for numerically approximating a root, applying it by hand for an iteration or two, and knowing when it fails.

questions.q: Newton's method is used to approximate a root of f(x) = x³ − 2x − 5 starting at x₀ = 2. Write the iteration formula and find x₁.
answer: x_(n+1) = x_n − f(x_n)/f′(x_n), with f′(x) = 3x² − 2.
The method fails if f′(x_n) = 0, or may diverge from a poor starting value.

points.title: Limits, continuity and differentiability
points.detail: The graphical treatment — recognising where a function is continuous but not differentiable, and what a limit means at a point.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a function being continuous at a point and being differentiable at that point, and give an example of a function that is one but not the other.
answer: Continuous at x = a: there is no break — the limit as x → a equals f(a).
Differentiable at x = a: the gradient approaching from the left equals that from the right.
f(x) = |x| is continuous at x = 0 but not differentiable — the gradient jumps from −1 to 1.
Differentiability implies continuity, but not the reverse.

points.title: Differentiation from first principles
points.detail: The limit definition of the derivative, and applying it to simple functions by hand.

questions.q: Use first principles to find the derivative of f(x) = x² + 3x.
answer: f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h
= lim [((x+h)² + 3(x+h)) − (x² + 3x)]/h = lim [2xh + h² + 3h]/h
= lim (2x + h + 3) as h → 0

points.title: Deducing the graph of the derivative
points.detail: Going from the graph of f to the graph of f′ — stationary points become x-intercepts, and the sign of the gradient sets the sign of f′.

questions.q: The graph of y = f(x) has a local maximum at x = −1, a local minimum at x = 3, and is increasing for x > 3. Describe the key features of the graph of y = f′(x).
answer: f′(x) = 0 at x = −1 and x = 3 — stationary points become x-intercepts of the derivative.
f′(x) > 0 for x < −1 and for x > 3 (f increasing).
f′(x) < 0 for −1 < x < 3 (f decreasing).
So the derivative graph cuts the axis downward at −1 and upward at 3.

points.title: Deducing the graph of an antiderivative
points.detail: Going the other way, from the graph of a function to the graph of one of its antiderivatives.

questions.q: The graph of y = f(x) is a straight line with a constant positive gradient. Describe the shape of the graph of an antiderivative of f, and explain why there are infinitely many.
answer: If f is linear, an antiderivative is quadratic — a parabola.
A positive gradient in f means the antiderivative is concave up.
Antiderivatives differ by an arbitrary constant c, which translates the graph vertically.
Infinitely many because any value of c satisfies F′(x) = f(x).

points.title: Standard derivatives
points.detail: Derivatives of xⁿ for n ∈ Q, eˣ, logₑ(x), sin(x), cos(x) and tan(x).

questions.q: Differentiate each: y = x^(3/2), y = log_e(x), y = tan(x).
answer: d/dx of log_e(x) = 1/x.
d/dx of tan(x) = sec²(x), equivalently 1/cos²(x).

points.title: Sum, difference and constant multiple rules
points.detail: Differentiating linear combinations of the standard functions.

questions.q: Differentiate y = 4x³ − 5e^x + 2log_e(x).
answer: dy/dx = 12x² − 5e^x + 2/x.
Each term differentiated separately; constants multiply through.

points.title: The product rule
points.detail: Applied by hand to simple combinations of polynomial, exponential, circular, logarithmic and power functions.

questions.q: Find dy/dx for y = x² sin(x), and evaluate it at x = π.
answer: Product rule: dy/dx = 2x sin(x) + x² cos(x).
At x = π: sin(π) = 0, cos(π) = −1.
dy/dx = 0 + π²(−1) = −π².
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 1, Q1 — differentiation requiring product and chain rules.

points.title: The quotient rule
points.detail: Applied by hand, including recognising when rearranging first is quicker.

questions.q: Find the derivative of y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) and state the value of x for which it is undefined.
answer: Quotient rule: [(2)(x − 3) − (2x + 1)(1)] / (x − 3)²
Undefined at x = 3, where the original function has a vertical asymptote.

points.title: The chain rule
points.detail: Differentiating composite functions, including nested transformations of the standard functions.

questions.q: Find the gradient of the tangent to y = (3x² − 1)⁴ at x = 1.
answer: Chain rule: dy/dx = 4(3x² − 1)³ × 6x = 24x(3x² − 1)³.

points.title: Graph sketching using differentiation
points.detail: Locating stationary points and determining their nature, finding points of inflection, and identifying intervals where a function is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.

questions.q: For f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 1, find the stationary points and determine the nature of each.
answer: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x − 2), so stationary at x = 0 and x = 2.
f″(x) = 6x − 6. At x = 0, f″ = −6 < 0 → local maximum (0, 1).
At x = 2, f″ = 6 > 0 → local minimum (2, −3).

points.title: Optimisation
points.detail: Local maximum and minimum values over an interval, applied to problems in context — including checking the endpoints of the interval, which is where marks are usually lost.

questions.q: A rectangular pen is built against a wall using 40 m of fencing on three sides. Find the dimensions giving the maximum area, and state the maximum area.
answer: Let the two equal sides be x and the third be 40 − 2x. Area A = x(40 − 2x) = 40x − 2x².
Second derivative is −4 < 0, confirming a maximum.
Dimensions 10 m by 20 m, maximum area 200 m². Check endpoints x = 0 and x = 20 both give A = 0.

points.title: Tangents, normals and rates of change
points.detail: The gradient of a tangent at a point, the equation of a tangent or normal, and interpreting the derivative as a rate of change in context.

questions.q: Find the equation of the tangent to y = x² − 2x at the point where x = 3, and the equation of the normal at the same point.
answer: y(3) = 9 − 6 = 3, so the point is (3, 3).
dy/dx = 2x − 2, so the gradient at x = 3 is 4.
Tangent: y − 3 = 4(x − 3), i.e. y = 4x − 9.
Normal gradient = −1/4, so y − 3 = −¼(x − 3), i.e. y = −x/4 + 15/4.

points.title: Antiderivatives
points.detail: Antiderivatives of polynomial and power functions, and of f(ax + b) where f is xⁿ for n ∈ Q, eˣ, sin(x) or cos(x), plus linear combinations of these.

questions.q: Find the antiderivative of f(x) = 6x² + e^(2x) − sin(3x).
answer: Antiderivative of 6x² is 2x³.
Antiderivative of e^(2x) is ½e^(2x).
Antiderivative of −sin(3x) is (1/3)cos(3x).
F(x) = 2x³ + ½e^(2x) + (1/3)cos(3x) + c — do not omit the constant.

points.title: The definite integral as a limiting sum
points.detail: Informal treatment of the integral as a limit of a sum, and approximating a definite integral using the trapezium rule.

questions.q: Use the trapezium rule with two intervals of equal width to estimate the area under y = x² between x = 0 and x = 2, and state whether the estimate is an over- or underestimate.
answer: Interval width h = 1; values y(0) = 0, y(1) = 1, y(2) = 4.
The exact value is 8/3 ≈ 2.67.
It is an overestimate because y = x² is concave up, so each chord lies above the curve.
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 2, Q6 — the trapezium rule with two trapeziums.

points.title: The fundamental theorem of calculus
points.detail: The link between antidifferentiation and the definite integral, and the properties of definite integrals.

questions.q: State the fundamental theorem of calculus and use it to evaluate the definite integral of 3x² from x = 1 to x = 3.
answer: If F is an antiderivative of f, then the definite integral of f from a to b equals F(b) − F(a).
An antiderivative of 3x² is x³.

points.title: Area under and between curves
points.detail: Finding the area of a region bounded by lines or curves over a specified interval, including handling signed area where the curve crosses the axis.

questions.q: Find the area of the region enclosed between y = x² and y = 2x.
answer: Intersections: x² = 2x gives x(x − 2) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 2.
Between these, 2x lies above x², so integrate (2x − x²) from 0 to 2.
Antiderivative: x² − x³/3, evaluated 0 to 2 gives 4 − 8/3.
Area = 4/3 square units.

points.title: Average value of a function
points.detail: The definition and its calculation over an interval.

questions.q: Find the average value of f(x) = x² over the interval [0, 3].
answer: Average value = 1/(b − a) × the definite integral of f from a to b.
Note this is not the same as the average of the endpoint values.

points.title: Applications of integration
points.detail: Problems in context, including the use of integration with probability density functions for continuous random variables.

questions.q: A particle's velocity is v(t) = 3t² − 12 m s⁻¹. Find the displacement from t = 0 to t = 4, and explain why this differs from the distance travelled.
answer: Displacement = integral of v from 0 to 4 = [t³ − 12t] from 0 to 4 = 64 − 48 = 16 m.
v = 0 when 3t² = 12, so t = 2. The particle moves backwards for 0 < t < 2.
Distance requires integrating |v|: |−16| from 0 to 2, plus 32 from 2 to 4, giving 48 m.
Displacement counts direction; distance does not.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Random variables
points.detail: The concept of a random variable, discrete versus continuous, and what a probability distribution specifies.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a discrete and a continuous random variable, giving one example of each from a school context.
answer: Discrete: takes countable, separate values — the number of students absent in a class.
Continuous: takes any value in an interval — the time a student takes to run 100 m.
Probability for a continuous variable is found over an interval, never at a single point.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Discrete probability distributions
points.detail: Specification by rule, table or graph; the probability mass function; and the requirement that the probabilities sum to one.

questions.q: A discrete random variable has Pr(X = 1) = 0.2, Pr(X = 2) = 3k, Pr(X = 3) = 0.3 and Pr(X = 4) = k. Find k.
answer: All probabilities must sum to 1.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Mean, variance and standard deviation of a discrete random variable
points.detail: Calculating E(X), Var(X) and sd(X), and interpreting each in the context of the distribution.

questions.q: For X with Pr(X = 0) = 0.4, Pr(X = 1) = 0.4 and Pr(X = 2) = 0.2, find E(X) and sd(X).

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Bernoulli trials
points.detail: The conditions that define them, and recognising whether a described situation actually satisfies those conditions.

questions.q: State the four conditions required for a sequence of Bernoulli trials, and explain whether drawing three cards from a deck without replacement satisfies them.
answer: Two outcomes per trial; a fixed number of trials; constant probability of success; trials independent.
Drawing without replacement changes the probability on each draw.
Trials are therefore not independent and p is not constant — not Bernoulli trials.
With replacement, it would satisfy all four.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: The binomial distribution
points.detail: Pr(X = x) = ⁿCₓ pˣ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ, mean np and variance np(1 − p), and how changing n or p changes the shape of the distribution.

questions.q: For X ~ Bi(8, 0.3), find Pr(X = 3), the mean and the variance.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Applying the binomial distribution
points.detail: Including 'at least' and 'at most' phrasing, conditional probability, and finding the smallest n that meets a stated condition.

questions.q: A machine produces items with a 5% defect rate. In a random sample of 20 items, find the probability that at least two are defective, and the mean number of defective items.
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 1, Q6 — variance and a cumulative probability for a binomial variable.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Continuous random variables and probability density functions
points.detail: The requirements that f(x) ≥ 0 and the total area equals one, and Pr(a < X < b) as a definite integral.

questions.q: A continuous random variable has f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4 and zero elsewhere. Find k, then find Pr(1 < X < 2).
answer: Total area must equal 1: the integral of kx from 0 to 4 = k[x²/2] = 8k = 1, so k = 1/8.
Pr(1 < X < 2) = integral of x/8 from 1 to 2 = [x²/16] from 1 to 2.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Measures for a continuous random variable
points.detail: Mean, median, percentiles, variance and standard deviation, and setting up the integral that each one requires.

questions.q: For the probability density function f(x) = x/8 on [0, 4], find the mean and the median.
answer: Mean = integral of x·f(x) from 0 to 4 = integral of x²/8 = [x³/24] from 0 to 4 = 64/24 = 8/3 ≈ 2.67.
Median m satisfies the integral of f from 0 to m = 0.5.
[x²/16] from 0 to m = m²/16 = 0.5, so m² = 8.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: The normal distribution
points.detail: Its shape and symmetry, the effect of μ and σ, and the approximate 68–95–99.7 proportions within one, two and three standard deviations.

questions.q: For X ~ N(60, 5²), use the 68–95–99.7 rule to state the percentage of values between 50 and 65, without standardising.
answer: 50 is 2 standard deviations below the mean; 65 is 1 above.
Between −2 sd and the mean: 95/2 = 47.5%.
Between the mean and +1 sd: 68/2 = 34%.
Total = 81.5%.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Standardising and finding normal probabilities
points.detail: Z = (X − μ)/σ, the standard normal distribution, and using technology to find probabilities or to work backwards from a probability to a value.

questions.q: For X ~ N(70, 8²), find Pr(X > 82) using standardisation, and state the z-score involved.
answer: Roughly consistent with the 95% rule: about 2.5% lie beyond z = 2.
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 2, Q12 — working backwards from normal probabilities to the mean.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Random sampling and the sample proportion
points.detail: Sample proportion p̂ defined as a random variable, and how it varies from sample to sample.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by saying the sample proportion is a random variable, and state the mean and standard deviation of its distribution for samples of size n from a population with proportion p.
answer: Each random sample gives a different value of p̂, so p̂ varies according to a probability distribution.
Mean of the distribution of p̂ = p.
Standard deviation = √(p(1 − p)/n).
Increasing n decreases the standard deviation, so estimates cluster more tightly around p.
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 2, Q8 — a random sample of n households estimating a population proportion.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: The distribution of sample proportions
points.detail: Mean p and standard deviation √(p(1 − p)/n), and simulating repeated random sampling to see the distribution form.

questions.q: A population has p = 0.4. For samples of size 100, state the mean and standard deviation of the distribution of sample proportions, and describe its shape.
answer: Mean = p = 0.4.
For large n the distribution of p̂ is approximately normal.
So about 95% of sample proportions fall within roughly 0.30 to 0.50.

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Confidence intervals for a population proportion
points.detail: The approximate interval from a large sample, the role of the quantile z, and the 95% interval as the case where z ≈ 1.96.

questions.q: In a sample of 200 voters, 96 support a proposal. Construct an approximate 95% confidence interval for the population proportion.
answer: Interval is (0.411, 0.549).

points.area: Area of Study 4 — Data analysis, probability and statistics
points.title: Interpreting a confidence interval
points.detail: What the interval actually claims, how intervals vary between samples, and why a wider interval is not automatically a worse one.

questions.q: A 95% confidence interval for a population proportion is (0.38, 0.46). Explain what this does and does not tell you.
answer: It is a plausible range for the population proportion based on this one sample.
'95%' refers to the method: about 95% of intervals built this way from repeated samples would capture the true p.
It does NOT mean there is a 95% probability that p lies in this particular interval — p is fixed, the interval varies.
A different sample would give a different interval.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Algorithm design
points.detail: Sequencing, decision-making and repetition as the building blocks, and representing the ordered steps of a mathematical process.

questions.q: Trace the following and state the values printed in order: n ← 20; k ← 6; while n > k do n ← n − k; print n; end while.
answer: First pass: n = 20 − 6 = 14, print 14. 14 > 6, continue.
Second pass: n = 8, print 8. 8 > 6, continue.
Third pass: n = 2, print 2. 2 > 6 is false, loop ends.
Printed: 14, 8, 2.
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 2, Q7 — tracing a while loop and listing the printed values.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Pseudocode
points.detail: Reading pseudocode and tracing what it produces, and writing it for a process such as Newton's method or the bisection method.

questions.q: Write pseudocode that repeatedly halves a positive number n until it is less than 1, printing the count of halvings performed.
answer: count ← 0
while n ≥ 1 do: n ← n/2; count ← count + 1; end while
print count
A pre-test loop is correct here — if n < 1 initially, the answer should be 0 halvings.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Examples, counter-examples and general cases
points.detail: Their role in working mathematically — a single counter-example disproves, an example never proves.

questions.q: A student claims 'for all real x, x² > x'. Provide a counter-example and explain what a counter-example establishes.
answer: Take x = 0.5: x² = 0.25, which is not greater than 0.5.
A single counter-example disproves a universal claim.
No number of supporting examples can prove such a claim — only a general argument can.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Exact versus approximate results
points.detail: Recognising which form technology has given you, and rounding to a stated number of decimal places or significant figures.

questions.q: A CAS returns 0.6931472 as the solution of e^x = 2. State the exact solution and explain when an approximate answer is acceptable.
answer: Exact solution: x = log_e(2).
An approximation is acceptable only when the question asks for a decimal answer, or specifies decimal places or significant figures.
Exam 1 is technology-free and almost always requires exact form.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Domain and range when graphing with technology
points.detail: Setting a window that actually shows the key features, and specifying domain restrictions correctly.

questions.q: A student graphs y = 1/(x − 2) on technology and reports that the graph 'has a vertical line at x = 2'. Explain the error and how to set the graph up correctly.
answer: The near-vertical line is a rendering artefact — the technology joins points either side of the asymptote.
There is no point on the graph at x = 2; the function is undefined there.
Set the domain to exclude x = 2, or use a graph style that does not connect across the discontinuity.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Parameters and families of functions
points.detail: The role of a parameter in the general form of a function or equation, and generating families of graphs to see its effect.

questions.q: For the family of functions y = a(x − 2)² + 1 where a ∈ R \ {0}, state which features are fixed and which change as a varies.
answer: Fixed: the turning point is always (2, 1); the axis of symmetry is always x = 2.
Changes: the width of the parabola, and whether it opens up (a > 0) or down (a < 0).
Number of x-intercepts changes: none if a > 0, two if a < 0.
questions.source: 2025 Methods Exam 1, Q9 — solutions depending on a parameter w.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Numerical, graphical and symbolic forms
points.detail: Linking the three representations of the same function or equation, and matching features across them.

questions.q: A function has a numerical table showing a sign change between x = 1 and x = 2, a graph crossing the x-axis once in that interval, and the rule f(x) = x³ − 3x − 1. Explain how the three representations agree.
answer: The sign change in the table indicates f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs.
The graph crossing the axis is that same root shown visually.
The rule can be used with Newton's method or a CAS solver to locate the root numerically.
All three describe the same fact: a solution of f(x) = 0 lies between 1 and 2.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Choosing and justifying CAS functionality
points.detail: Selecting the right tool for the task, applying suitable constraints and conditions, and verifying the result rather than trusting it.

questions.q: A student uses a CAS 'solve' command and obtains an answer of 1.4142136. Explain what has gone wrong if an exact answer was required, and how to obtain one.
answer: The technology has returned a decimal approximation rather than an exact value.
The exact answer is √2.
Set the CAS to exact or auto mode, or use an exact-form solve command rather than a numerical solver.

points.area: Across the course — modelling, algorithms and technology
points.title: Communicating mathematical reasoning
points.detail: Setting out the stages — formulation, solution, interpretation — so the working can be followed, which is what the modelling and problem-solving tasks are marked on.

questions.q: A student writes only '= 24' as their answer to a four-mark problem and receives one mark. Explain what was missing and what a full response requires.
answer: The reasoning is absent — marks are allocated to the stages of the solution, not only the final value.
Required: the relationship or rule being used, the substitution, the working, then the answer.
The answer should be stated in context with units where relevant.

papers: VCAA 2023–2026 Methods examinations plus NHT papers, and commercial trial exams, in your Methods folder. Exam 1 is technology-free; Exam 2 is 20 multiple-choice plus extended answer.

name: Physics
areas: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity

points.title: Aims, questions, hypotheses and predictions
points.detail: Constructing an aim and a research question; identifying the independent, dependent and controlled variables; writing a hypothesis that can actually be tested; predicting possible outcomes.

questions.q: A student investigates how the drop height of a ball affects its rebound height. Write a testable hypothesis and identify the independent and dependent variables.
answer: Hypothesis: as the drop height increases, the rebound height will increase proportionally.
Independent variable: drop height.
Dependent variable: rebound height.
