questions.q: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. Write a testable hypothesis and identify the independent and dependent variables.
answer: Hypothesis: as temperature increases towards the optimum, the rate of reaction will increase, then fall sharply above the optimum as the enzyme denatures.
Independent variable: temperature of the reaction mixture.
Dependent variable: rate of reaction, for example volume of product formed per minute.
A hypothesis must be a testable prediction about a relationship, not a restatement of the aim.

points.title: Scientific methodologies
points.detail: Distinguishing controlled experiment, correlational study, classification and identification, fieldwork, modelling, simulation, literature review, product or process development, and case study, and choosing the one that suits a question.

questions.q: Researchers compare lung cancer rates in smokers and non-smokers using existing hospital records. Name the methodology and explain why a causal claim cannot be made.
answer: Methodology: a correlational study.
The independent variable was not manipulated by the researchers and participants were not randomly allocated.
Uncontrolled extraneous variables could explain the relationship, so only an association can be claimed.

points.title: Accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility and validity
points.detail: Accuracy is closeness to a true value; precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other; repeatability is the same team repeating the same method; reproducibility is a different team or method; validity is whether the investigation actually tests the hypothesis.

questions.q: Five readings of a solution's concentration cluster tightly but all sit well above the known value. Describe the precision and accuracy of these results, and suggest a likely cause.
answer: The results are precise because the repeated readings are close to one another.
The results are not accurate because they are consistently far from the known true value.
A systematic error such as an uncalibrated instrument would produce this pattern.

points.title: Errors, outliers and uncertainty
points.detail: Random errors scatter data and are reduced by repeat trials and averaging; systematic errors shift every reading in one direction and are reduced by calibration; personal errors are mistakes. Outliers are identified, reported and only excluded with justification.

questions.q: Explain why repeating a measurement many times reduces the effect of random error but not systematic error.
answer: Random errors vary unpredictably in size and direction, so they tend to cancel when many readings are averaged.
Systematic errors shift every reading in the same direction by a similar amount, so averaging preserves the shift.
Systematic error is addressed by calibrating or changing the instrument or method.

points.title: Controls, control groups and sample size
points.detail: The difference between a controlled variable and a control group; the purpose of a control group as a comparison; why larger samples and random allocation reduce the influence of individual variation.

questions.q: Distinguish between a controlled variable and a control group, using an example from a plant growth experiment.
answer: A controlled variable is a factor kept constant across all groups, such as light intensity or pot size.
A control group is a group that does not receive the experimental treatment, such as plants given water with no fertiliser.
The control group provides the baseline that treated groups are compared against.

points.title: Presenting and analysing data
points.detail: Choosing an appropriate table or graph; independent variable on the horizontal axis; using line graphs for continuous data and column graphs for discrete categories; describing trends, patterns and relationships rather than restating every value.

questions.q: A student measures oxygen produced by pondweed at six light intensities. State the graph type they should use and justify the choice.
answer: A line graph should be used.
Both light intensity and oxygen produced are continuous numerical variables, so intermediate values are meaningful.
Light intensity, the independent variable, goes on the horizontal axis.

points.title: Conclusions, limitations and evaluation
points.detail: Writing a conclusion that refers to the hypothesis and the data, and evaluating limitations of the method, sample and measurement before suggesting improvements.

questions.q: A conclusion states that a drug 'cures' a disease after a trial on 12 people with no control group. Identify two problems and state how the conclusion should be qualified.
answer: The sample size of 12 is too small to generalise to a population.
Without a control group there is no comparison, so improvement could be due to a placebo effect or natural recovery.
The conclusion should be limited to the sample tested and should describe an association rather than a cure.

points.title: Ethical concepts and ethical understandings
points.detail: Beneficence, integrity, justice, non-maleficence and respect, and how they apply to biological research involving humans, animals, tissue samples and genetic information.

questions.q: A company wants to store DNA samples from a trial and reuse them in future unrelated research. Identify two ethical concepts at stake and explain how each applies.
answer: Respect: participants' autonomy requires informed consent for each use of their genetic material, not blanket consent.
Non-maleficence: reuse could expose participants to harm such as discrimination or loss of privacy.
Integrity would also require the company to disclose honestly how the samples will be used and stored.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Structure of DNA
points.detail: Nucleotide subunits of deoxyribose, phosphate and a base; the antiparallel double helix; complementary base pairing of A with T and G with C by hydrogen bonds; the sugar-phosphate backbone.

questions.q: Describe the structure of a DNA molecule, referring to nucleotides, the bonding between strands and the orientation of the strands.
answer: Each nucleotide consists of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and one of four nitrogenous bases.
Nucleotides join by covalent bonds between the sugar of one and the phosphate of the next, forming a sugar-phosphate backbone.
The two strands are antiparallel and are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, A with T and G with C.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Chromosomes, histones and chromatin
points.detail: How DNA is wound around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which coil into chromatin and condense into chromosomes; why packaging matters for storage and for access during transcription.

questions.q: Explain the role of histone proteins in eukaryotic cells.
answer: DNA wraps around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which allows a very long molecule to be packaged into the nucleus.
The tightness of this packaging affects whether genes can be accessed by transcription machinery, so histones also contribute to gene regulation.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Genome, gene and proteome
points.detail: The genome as all the genetic material of an organism, a gene as a segment coding for a functional product, and the proteome as all the proteins expressed by a cell or organism at a given time.

questions.q: Two cells in the same person have identical genomes but different proteomes. Explain how this is possible.
answer: Every body cell contains the same DNA because it is derived from the same zygote by mitosis.
Different genes are switched on or off in different cell types, so different proteins are transcribed and translated.
The proteome is also affected by alternative splicing and post-translational modification, and it changes over time.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Gene structure in prokaryotes and eukaryotes
points.detail: Promoter, coding region and terminator; operator and operon organisation in prokaryotes; exons and introns in eukaryotes; why prokaryotic genes are continuous.

questions.q: State one structural difference between a typical prokaryotic gene and a typical eukaryotic gene, and one consequence of that difference.
answer: Eukaryotic genes contain non-coding introns between coding exons, while prokaryotic coding regions are continuous.
As a consequence, eukaryotic pre-mRNA must be spliced before translation, whereas prokaryotic mRNA can be translated immediately.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: RNA structure and types
points.detail: Single-stranded RNA with ribose and uracil; the roles of mRNA as the transcript, tRNA as the amino acid carrier with an anticodon, and rRNA as part of the ribosome.

questions.q: Compare the structure of DNA and mRNA, and state the function of tRNA.
answer: DNA is double stranded and contains deoxyribose and thymine; mRNA is single stranded and contains ribose and uracil.
DNA is much longer and remains in the nucleus, while mRNA is short and moves to the cytosol.
tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that base-pairs with the complementary mRNA codon during translation.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Transcription
points.detail: RNA polymerase binding at the promoter, unwinding the helix, reading the template strand and building pre-mRNA from complementary free nucleotides until the terminator is reached.

questions.q: Outline the process of transcription in a eukaryotic cell.
answer: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter region of the gene and unwinds the DNA double helix.
Free RNA nucleotides are joined in a complementary sequence against the template strand, with uracil pairing to adenine.
The enzyme reaches the terminator, the pre-mRNA transcript is released and the DNA rewinds.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: RNA processing and alternative splicing
points.detail: Addition of a methylated cap and a poly-A tail, removal of introns and splicing of exons; alternative splicing producing several mature mRNAs and therefore several proteins from one gene.

questions.q: Explain how one gene can give rise to more than one protein in a eukaryotic cell.
answer: Pre-mRNA contains both exons and introns, and introns are removed during RNA processing.
In alternative splicing, different combinations of exons are joined together to produce different mature mRNA molecules.
Each mature mRNA is translated into a polypeptide with a different amino acid sequence, so one gene yields several proteins.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: The genetic code
points.detail: Triplet codons read from mRNA; the code as degenerate, non-overlapping and near universal; the start codon AUG and the three stop codons; reading a codon table.

questions.q: The genetic code is described as degenerate and universal. Explain what each term means and give one consequence of universality.
answer: Degenerate means most amino acids are specified by more than one codon, so some base substitutions do not change the amino acid.
Universal means the same codons specify the same amino acids in nearly all organisms.
A consequence is that a human gene inserted into a bacterium produces the same protein, which makes recombinant technology possible.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Translation
points.detail: Initiation at the start codon, tRNA anticodons pairing with codons in the ribosome, peptide bond formation, translocation and termination at a stop codon.

questions.q: Describe the process of translation from the arrival of mRNA in the cytosol to the release of a polypeptide.
answer: The mRNA binds to a ribosome and the ribosome moves to the start codon AUG.
A tRNA with the complementary anticodon delivers its amino acid to the ribosome.
A peptide bond forms between adjacent amino acids and the ribosome translocates one codon along the mRNA.
When a stop codon is reached no tRNA binds, and the completed polypeptide is released.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Amino acids and levels of protein structure
points.detail: Amino acid structure and the twenty amino acids; primary sequence, secondary helices and sheets, tertiary folding from R group interactions, and quaternary association of subunits.

questions.q: A single base substitution changes one amino acid in a protein and the protein no longer functions. Explain how this occurs.
answer: The primary structure determines how the chain folds, because interactions between R groups set the tertiary structure.
Changing one amino acid can alter or remove an interaction, so the protein folds into a different three-dimensional shape.
The active or binding site is no longer complementary to its substrate or target, so function is lost.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: The protein secretory pathway
points.detail: Nucleus, ribosome, rough endoplasmic reticulum, transport vesicle, Golgi apparatus, secretory vesicle and plasma membrane, and the modification that occurs at each stage.

questions.q: Trace the path of a protein that is exported from a cell, naming the organelles involved and what happens at each.
answer: mRNA is transcribed in the nucleus and moves through a nuclear pore to a ribosome on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
The polypeptide is synthesised into the rough endoplasmic reticulum, where initial folding occurs.
A transport vesicle buds off and carries the protein to the Golgi apparatus, where it is further modified and packaged.
A secretory vesicle carries the protein to the plasma membrane and releases it by exocytosis.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Functional diversity of proteins
points.detail: Structural, enzymatic, transport, receptor, hormonal, immunological and contractile roles, with the link between shape and function in each case.

questions.q: Using two named examples, explain how the shape of a protein relates to its function.
answer: Haemoglobin has a quaternary structure with haem groups shaped to bind oxygen reversibly for transport.
An antibody has a Y shape with variable regions complementary to one specific antigen, allowing specific binding.
In both cases a precise three-dimensional shape creates a binding site that fits one kind of molecule.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Gene regulation and the trp operon
points.detail: Repressible operons; the roles of the regulatory gene, repressor protein, operator and structural genes; how tryptophan acts as a corepressor to switch the operon off.

questions.q: Explain what happens to the trp operon when tryptophan levels in a bacterial cell rise.
answer: Tryptophan acts as a corepressor and binds to the repressor protein produced by the regulatory gene.
The activated repressor changes shape and binds to the operator region.
RNA polymerase can no longer transcribe the structural genes, so the enzymes for tryptophan synthesis are not made and resources are conserved.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Enzymes used to manipulate DNA
points.detail: Restriction endonucleases cutting at recognition sites to give sticky or blunt ends, DNA ligase joining fragments, and DNA polymerase extending a strand from a primer.

questions.q: Explain why sticky ends are more useful than blunt ends when a gene is inserted into a plasmid.
answer: Sticky ends are short single-stranded overhangs produced by a staggered cut.
If the plasmid and the gene are cut with the same restriction enzyme, their overhangs are complementary and pair by hydrogen bonding.
This holds the fragments in place and in the correct orientation so DNA ligase can seal the sugar-phosphate backbone, which is more efficient than joining blunt ends.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Polymerase chain reaction
points.detail: Denaturation, annealing of primers and extension by heat-stable polymerase; the role of temperature at each step; exponential amplification of a target sequence.

questions.q: Describe the three steps of one PCR cycle and state the temperature change that drives each.
answer: Denaturation at around 95 degrees Celsius breaks the hydrogen bonds and separates the two DNA strands.
Annealing at around 50 to 60 degrees Celsius allows primers to bind to the complementary sequences flanking the target region.
Extension at around 72 degrees Celsius allows heat-stable DNA polymerase to add free nucleotides and build new complementary strands.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Gel electrophoresis
points.detail: Separation of fragments by size through a gel under an electric field; movement of the negatively charged DNA towards the positive electrode; use of a size standard to estimate fragment lengths.

questions.q: Explain why DNA fragments separate into bands during gel electrophoresis and how fragment size is determined.
answer: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so it migrates towards the positive electrode.
Smaller fragments pass through the pores of the gel more easily and travel further than larger fragments in the same time.
Distances travelled are compared with a standard ladder of known fragment sizes to estimate the size of each band.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Recombinant plasmids and bacterial transformation
points.detail: Plasmids as vectors, insertion of a gene of interest, transformation of bacteria and the use of antibiotic-resistance or marker genes to select transformed cells.

questions.q: Outline how bacteria can be made to produce human insulin.
answer: The human insulin gene is isolated and cut out using a restriction enzyme, and a plasmid is cut with the same enzyme.
DNA ligase joins the gene into the plasmid to form a recombinant plasmid, which is taken up by bacteria during transformation.
Transformed bacteria are selected using a marker gene and then cultured, transcribing and translating the gene to produce insulin.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing
points.detail: Guide RNA directing the Cas9 nuclease to a complementary target sequence, the double-strand cut, and repair that disables a gene or inserts a new sequence.

questions.q: Explain how the CRISPR-Cas9 system edits a specific gene and why it is described as precise.
answer: A guide RNA is designed to be complementary to the target DNA sequence and directs the Cas9 enzyme to that site.
Cas9 makes a double-stranded cut at that location.
The cell's repair machinery may disable the gene or insert a supplied sequence; precision comes from the guide RNA binding only to a matching sequence.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Transgenic and genetically modified organisms
points.detail: The difference between a genetically modified and a transgenic organism; agricultural, medical and industrial applications; benefits and risks to be weighed.

questions.q: Distinguish between a genetically modified organism and a transgenic organism, and give one example of a transgenic organism.
answer: A genetically modified organism has had its genome altered in any way, including the removal or alteration of its own genes.
A transgenic organism specifically contains a gene from a different species.
Bt cotton, which carries a bacterial gene for an insecticidal protein, is an example of a transgenic organism.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Nucleic acids and proteins
points.title: Social and ethical implications of genetic technologies
points.detail: Consent, privacy of genetic information, access and equity, ecological risk, and the use of ethical concepts to weigh competing interests in gene technology debates.

questions.q: A new gene therapy is extremely effective but extremely expensive. Use two ethical concepts to discuss whether it should be publicly funded.
answer: Justice requires fair distribution of benefits and burdens, so a treatment available only to the wealthy raises equity concerns.
Beneficence supports funding because the therapy produces substantial benefit for patients.
A reasoned position must weigh the opportunity cost of directing limited public funds away from other treatments.

points.title: Enzymes and activation energy
points.detail: Enzymes as biological catalysts that lower activation energy without being consumed, allowing reactions to proceed at body temperature and at useful rates.

questions.q: Explain how an enzyme increases the rate of a reaction, referring to activation energy.
answer: The enzyme binds the substrate at its active site and stabilises the transition state.
This lowers the activation energy needed for the reaction to proceed.
A greater proportion of collisions therefore have sufficient energy to react, so the rate increases; the enzyme is unchanged and can be reused.

points.title: Models of enzyme action and specificity
points.detail: The lock-and-key model and the induced fit model; why an active site is complementary to only one substrate or a small group of similar substrates.

questions.q: Describe the induced fit model and explain how it differs from the lock-and-key model.
answer: In the induced fit model the active site is flexible and changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, creating a closer fit.
In the lock-and-key model the active site is a rigid shape exactly complementary to the substrate.
Induced fit better explains how binding strains bonds in the substrate and how some enzymes act on several similar substrates.

points.title: Coenzymes and cofactors
points.detail: Roles of NAD plus, NADP plus, FAD and coenzyme A in carrying hydrogen ions, electrons or acetyl groups between stages of photosynthesis and respiration.

questions.q: Explain the role of NAD plus in cellular respiration and why the cell must regenerate it.
answer: NAD plus is a coenzyme that accepts hydrogen ions and electrons released during glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, becoming NADH.
NADH carries these electrons to the electron transport chain, where their energy is used to make ATP.
If NAD plus is not regenerated, glycolysis and the Krebs cycle stall because there is no acceptor for the released electrons.

points.title: Factors affecting enzyme activity
points.detail: The effect of temperature, pH, substrate concentration and enzyme concentration on rate, including optimum values, denaturation and saturation.

questions.q: Describe and explain the shape of a graph of reaction rate against substrate concentration at a fixed enzyme concentration.
answer: Rate increases steeply at low substrate concentration because more active sites are occupied as substrate is added.
The curve then levels off because all active sites are occupied and the enzyme is saturated.
Beyond this point, enzyme concentration rather than substrate concentration is the limiting factor.

points.title: Competitive and non-competitive inhibition
points.detail: Competitive inhibitors binding at the active site and being outcompeted by high substrate concentration; non-competitive inhibitors binding elsewhere and changing the shape of the active site.

questions.q: Distinguish between competitive and non-competitive inhibition, and explain how increasing substrate concentration affects each.
answer: A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate and binds to the active site, blocking substrate binding.
A non-competitive inhibitor binds at an allosteric site elsewhere, changing the shape of the active site so the substrate no longer fits.
Increasing substrate concentration reduces the effect of a competitive inhibitor but has little effect on non-competitive inhibition.

points.title: ATP and energy transfer
points.detail: ATP as the immediate energy currency of the cell, the release of energy when the terminal phosphate bond is hydrolysed to ADP and phosphate, and the regeneration of ATP by photosynthesis and respiration.

questions.q: Explain why cells use ATP rather than glucose directly as an energy source for cellular work.
answer: ATP releases a small, usable quantity of energy when it is hydrolysed to ADP and inorganic phosphate, which matches the requirement of individual reactions.
Glucose holds a large amount of energy that would be wasted or damaging if released in one step.
ATP can also be made and used rapidly anywhere in the cell, coupling energy-releasing to energy-requiring reactions.

points.title: Chloroplast structure and the overall equation
points.detail: Thylakoid membranes, grana and stroma; the balanced equation for photosynthesis; the location of each stage within the organelle.

questions.q: Write the overall balanced equation for photosynthesis and state where each stage occurs in the chloroplast.
answer: Six carbon dioxide plus six water, in the presence of light and chlorophyll, produces one glucose plus six oxygen.
The light-dependent stage occurs at the thylakoid membranes of the grana.
The light-independent stage occurs in the stroma.

points.title: The light-dependent stage
points.detail: Absorption of light by chlorophyll, photolysis of water releasing oxygen, and the production of ATP and NADPH for the next stage.

questions.q: State the inputs and outputs of the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis and explain the origin of the oxygen released.
answer: Inputs: light energy, water, ADP and inorganic phosphate, and NADP plus.
Outputs: ATP, NADPH and oxygen gas.
Oxygen comes from the photolysis of water, in which light energy splits water into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen.

points.title: The light-independent stage
points.detail: Carbon fixation by rubisco in the Calvin cycle, use of ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent stage, and the production of glucose in the stroma.

questions.q: Explain why the light-independent stage stops within minutes if a plant is placed in darkness, even though it does not use light directly.
answer: The light-independent stage requires ATP and NADPH, which are produced only by the light-dependent stage.
In darkness the light-dependent stage stops, so supplies of ATP and NADPH are quickly exhausted.
Without these inputs, carbon dioxide cannot be reduced and glucose production ceases.

points.title: Factors affecting the rate of photosynthesis
points.detail: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, water availability and temperature as limiting factors; interpreting plateau and decline on rate graphs.

questions.q: A graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity rises then plateaus. Explain the plateau and predict the effect of also raising the carbon dioxide concentration.
answer: At low light intensity, light is the limiting factor, so the rate rises as intensity increases.
At the plateau some other factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, has become limiting.
Increasing carbon dioxide would raise the plateau to a higher rate if carbon dioxide was the limiting factor.

points.title: C3, C4 and CAM plants
points.detail: Photorespiration in hot, dry conditions; the spatial separation of carbon fixation in C4 plants and the temporal separation in CAM plants as adaptations that limit water loss.

questions.q: Explain how the adaptation of CAM plants reduces water loss while still allowing carbon fixation.
answer: CAM plants open their stomata at night, when temperature is lower and humidity higher, so less water is lost by transpiration.
Carbon dioxide taken in at night is fixed and stored as an organic acid.
During the day the stomata close and the stored carbon dioxide is released for the Calvin cycle, which requires the light-dependent products.

points.title: Improving photosynthetic efficiency
points.detail: Agricultural and biotechnological strategies such as controlled environment cropping, carbon dioxide enrichment, altering rubisco and engineering C4 traits into C3 crops.

questions.q: Explain one biotechnological strategy used to increase crop yield through improved photosynthetic efficiency.
answer: Carbon dioxide enrichment in glasshouses raises the concentration above atmospheric levels so that carbon dioxide is no longer limiting.
This increases the rate of carbon fixation in the Calvin cycle and therefore glucose production and biomass.
Alternatives include engineering C4 traits into C3 crops to reduce losses from photorespiration.

points.title: Mitochondrial structure and the overall equation
points.detail: Outer and inner membranes, cristae and matrix; the balanced equation for aerobic cellular respiration; the location of each stage.

questions.q: Explain how the folded inner membrane of the mitochondrion supports the function of the organelle.
answer: The cristae greatly increase the surface area of the inner membrane.
The electron transport chain and ATP synthase are embedded in this membrane, so a larger area allows more of these proteins.
More electron transport chains means more ATP can be produced per unit time.

points.title: Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain
points.detail: Inputs, outputs, location and ATP yield of each stage of aerobic respiration, including the role of NADH and FADH2 in carrying electrons to the inner membrane.

questions.q: Name the location and the ATP yield of each of the three stages of aerobic cellular respiration.
answer: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol, splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules and yields a net two ATP plus two NADH.
The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, releases carbon dioxide and yields two ATP plus NADH and FADH2 per glucose.
The electron transport chain occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane and yields most of the ATP, around twenty-six to twenty-eight.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water, and the total yield is about thirty to thirty-two ATP per glucose.

points.title: Anaerobic fermentation
points.detail: Lactic acid fermentation in animal cells and ethanol fermentation in yeast and plants; why the ATP yield is only two per glucose; the regeneration of NAD plus.

questions.q: Compare anaerobic fermentation in a human muscle cell with anaerobic fermentation in yeast, including the products and ATP yield of each.
answer: In human muscle cells, pyruvate is converted to lactic acid and no carbon dioxide is released.
In yeast, pyruvate is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Both yield only two ATP per glucose because only glycolysis produces ATP; the conversion of pyruvate regenerates NAD plus so glycolysis can continue.

points.title: Biotechnological applications of respiration
points.detail: Anaerobic fermentation in brewing and baking, bioethanol production from crops and waste, and comparison of the energy inputs and outputs of biofuels.

questions.q: Explain how yeast is used to produce bioethanol and evaluate one advantage and one limitation of bioethanol as a fuel.
answer: Yeast ferments sugars from crops such as sugar cane or corn anaerobically, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide, and the ethanol is then distilled.
An advantage is that the crop absorbs carbon dioxide as it grows, so net carbon emissions are lower than for fossil fuels.
A limitation is that land, water and fertiliser used for fuel crops compete with food production, and processing itself requires energy.

points.title: Cellular and non-cellular pathogens
points.detail: Bacteria, fungi, protozoa and parasites as cellular pathogens; viruses and prions as non-cellular; how each causes disease.

questions.q: Distinguish between a cellular and a non-cellular pathogen, giving one example of each.
answer: A cellular pathogen is made of one or more cells and can reproduce independently, for example a bacterium such as Salmonella.
A non-cellular pathogen is not made of cells and must use a host cell to replicate, for example a virus such as influenza.
Prions are also non-cellular, being misfolded proteins that cause other proteins to misfold.

points.title: Antigens, self and non-self
points.detail: Antigens as molecules that trigger an immune response; self-antigens and MHC markers; how the immune system distinguishes self from non-self.

questions.q: Explain how the immune system distinguishes its own cells from a pathogen.
answer: Body cells display self-antigens, including MHC class I markers, which immune cells recognise as belonging to the organism.
Pathogens display non-self antigens on their surfaces that do not match the host markers.
Lymphocytes that would react against self-antigens are normally destroyed or inactivated during development, so only non-self antigens trigger a response.

points.title: Plant defences
points.detail: Physical barriers such as cuticle, bark and thorns; chemical defences such as toxins and antimicrobial compounds; localised responses such as galls and cell death at the infection site.

questions.q: Describe one physical and one chemical defence used by plants against pathogens.
answer: A physical defence is the waxy cuticle or bark, which prevents pathogens from entering the plant tissues.
A chemical defence is the production of toxins or antimicrobial compounds that kill or inhibit invading organisms.
Plants may also seal off infected tissue by killing surrounding cells to limit spread.

points.title: First line of defence in animals
points.detail: Skin, mucous membranes, cilia, stomach acid, lysozyme in tears and saliva, and the protective role of normal microbiota.

questions.q: Explain how the first line of defence prevents infection, referring to a physical, a chemical and a microbiological barrier.
answer: Physical: intact skin forms a barrier that pathogens cannot readily penetrate, and cilia sweep trapped pathogens out of the airways.
Chemical: stomach acid and lysozyme in tears and saliva destroy many pathogens before they can establish.
Microbiota: harmless resident bacteria compete with pathogens for nutrients and space, making colonisation more difficult.

points.title: Inflammation and the innate response
points.detail: Mast cells releasing histamine, vasodilation and increased permeability, the movement of phagocytes to the site, and the signs of inflammation.

questions.q: Describe the inflammatory response and explain how it helps to remove a pathogen.
answer: Damaged tissue and mast cells release histamine, which causes vasodilation and increases capillary permeability.
Increased blood flow causes redness, heat and swelling and delivers more plasma and leukocytes to the site.
Phagocytes move out of the capillaries into the tissue to engulf and destroy pathogens and debris.

points.title: Innate cells and chemicals
points.detail: Phagocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils, natural killer cells, the complement system, interferons and fever as non-specific defences.

questions.q: State the role of natural killer cells and of interferons in the innate immune response.
answer: Natural killer cells detect body cells with abnormal or absent MHC class I markers, such as virus-infected or cancerous cells, and trigger their death.
Interferons are released by virus-infected cells and signal neighbouring cells to increase their antiviral defences.
Both act non-specifically, without being tailored to a particular antigen, and do not produce memory.

points.title: The lymphatic system
points.detail: Lymph vessels, lymph nodes and lymphoid organs; the movement of antigen-presenting cells and lymphocytes; why nodes swell during infection.

questions.q: Explain the role of the lymphatic system in the immune response and why lymph nodes swell during an infection.
answer: Lymph collects fluid and pathogens from tissues and carries antigen-presenting cells to lymph nodes.
Lymph nodes contain large numbers of lymphocytes, so this is where antigen presentation and clonal selection occur.
Nodes swell because lymphocytes proliferate rapidly there during clonal expansion.

points.title: Third line of defence and immunological memory
points.detail: Specificity of the adaptive response, the lag before a primary response, and the faster, larger secondary response produced by memory cells.

questions.q: Compare the primary and secondary immune responses to the same antigen.
answer: The primary response has a lag of several days while clonal selection and expansion occur, and antibody concentration rises slowly to a lower peak.
The secondary response is faster because memory B and T cells specific to that antigen already exist.
Antibody concentration rises sooner, reaches a higher peak and is sustained longer, so symptoms may not develop.

points.title: Humoral immunity and antibodies
points.detail: B cell activation, clonal expansion into plasma cells and memory cells, antibody structure with variable and constant regions, and antibody actions such as agglutination and neutralisation.

questions.q: Describe the structure of an antibody and explain two ways antibodies help to eliminate a pathogen.
answer: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein with two variable regions at the tips that bind one specific antigen, and a constant region.
Antibodies can agglutinate pathogens by binding several at once, clumping them so phagocytes can engulf them more easily.
Antibodies can neutralise toxins or block a virus from attaching to host cells, and can mark pathogens for destruction by complement.

points.title: Cell-mediated immunity and antigen presentation
points.detail: Antigen-presenting cells, MHC class I and II, helper T cells activating B cells and cytotoxic T cells, and cytotoxic T cells destroying infected cells.

questions.q: Outline the sequence of events from a dendritic cell engulfing a virus to the destruction of virus-infected body cells.
answer: The dendritic cell engulfs the virus and presents fragments of viral antigen on its MHC class II markers.
It migrates to a lymph node where a helper T cell with a complementary receptor binds and is activated.
The activated helper T cell releases cytokines that stimulate the clonal expansion of cytotoxic T cells specific to that antigen.
Cytotoxic T cells recognise the viral antigen presented on MHC class I of infected body cells and trigger their death.

points.title: Natural, artificial, active and passive immunity
points.detail: Classifying immunity by how antigens or antibodies were acquired; the duration of protection in each case and the presence or absence of memory.

questions.q: Classify the immunity gained by an infant from breast milk and the immunity gained from a vaccination, and explain why they differ in duration.
answer: Breast milk provides natural passive immunity, because ready-made antibodies are transferred without the infant's immune system responding.
Vaccination provides artificial active immunity, because the infant's own immune system responds to introduced antigens.
Passive immunity is short-lived because the antibodies are broken down and no memory cells are produced, while active immunity is long-lasting because memory cells are formed.

points.title: Vaccines and herd immunity
points.detail: Vaccine composition, the primary response they induce, booster doses and the way high vaccination coverage protects those who cannot be vaccinated.

questions.q: Explain how herd immunity protects a child who is too immunocompromised to be vaccinated.
answer: When a high proportion of the population is immune, most contacts of an infected person are unable to be infected.
The chain of transmission is broken, so the pathogen circulates at a much lower level in the community.
The unvaccinated child is therefore much less likely to encounter an infectious person, even though they have no immunity themselves.

points.title: Allergies and autoimmune disease
points.detail: Allergy as a hypersensitive response to a harmless antigen involving IgE, mast cells and histamine; autoimmune disease as a failure of self-tolerance.

questions.q: Explain the difference between an allergic reaction and an autoimmune disease, and describe what happens in the body during an allergic response.
answer: An allergic reaction is an exaggerated immune response to a harmless non-self antigen such as pollen.
An autoimmune disease occurs when the immune system fails to recognise self-antigens and attacks the body's own tissues.
In an allergic response, IgE antibodies bind to mast cells and trigger the release of histamine, causing vasodilation, swelling, mucus production and, in severe cases, anaphylaxis.

points.title: Emerging pathogens, antigenic drift and shift
points.detail: Why new and re-emerging diseases appear, the accumulation of small mutations in antigenic drift and the reassortment of genetic material in antigenic shift.

questions.q: Explain why the influenza vaccine must be reformulated each year.
answer: Influenza viruses accumulate small mutations in their surface antigens through antigenic drift.
Memory cells and antibodies produced against last season's antigens no longer bind the altered antigens effectively.
The vaccine is therefore updated to match the strains predicted to circulate, so that a protective specific response is produced.

points.title: Monoclonal antibodies and immunotherapies
points.detail: Production of identical antibodies against a single antigen; use in diagnosis, targeted drug delivery and cancer treatment; the principle of rational drug design.

questions.q: Explain why monoclonal antibodies can deliver a cancer drug to tumour cells with fewer side effects than conventional chemotherapy.
answer: Monoclonal antibodies are identical and bind to one specific antigen found on the surface of the tumour cells.
A drug attached to the antibody is therefore delivered mainly to cells carrying that antigen.
Healthy cells lacking the antigen receive much less of the drug, so damage to normal dividing tissue is reduced.

points.title: Developing and evaluating treatments
points.detail: Preclinical testing and the phases of clinical trials, the roles of scientists, regulators and health organisations, and the use of controls and blinding in drug trials.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial when a new vaccine is tested.
answer: A placebo group provides a comparison so that any effect of the vaccine can be separated from natural variation and the placebo effect.
Double blinding means neither participants nor researchers know the allocation, which prevents expectation from biasing reported symptoms or assessments.
Together these features improve the validity of the conclusion that the vaccine caused the observed difference.

points.title: Types of mutation
points.detail: Point mutations including silent, missense and nonsense; block mutations such as deletion, duplication, inversion and translocation; frameshift effects of insertions and deletions.

questions.q: Explain why the insertion of a single base usually has a more severe effect on a protein than the substitution of a single base.
answer: An insertion shifts the reading frame, so every codon after the insertion point is altered.
This changes most of the amino acid sequence from that point on and may introduce a premature stop codon.
A substitution changes at most one codon, and because the code is degenerate it may not change the amino acid at all.

points.title: Somatic and germline mutations, and mutagens
points.detail: Which mutations can be inherited; physical, chemical and biological mutagens; why only germline mutations contribute to evolution.

questions.q: Explain why a somatic mutation caused by UV radiation does not contribute to the evolution of the species.
answer: A somatic mutation occurs in a body cell, not in a gamete or a cell that produces gametes.
It is therefore not passed to offspring and does not change allele frequencies in the next generation.
Only germline mutations are inherited and can be acted on by natural selection over generations.

points.title: Sources of genetic variation
points.detail: Mutation as the ultimate source of new alleles, and crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation as sources of new combinations.

questions.q: Describe three processes that generate genetic variation in a sexually reproducing population.
answer: Mutation introduces new alleles into the population and is the only source of entirely new genetic material.
Crossing over in prophase I exchanges segments between homologous chromosomes, producing new combinations of alleles.
Independent assortment in metaphase I and random fertilisation combine alleles in new ways in each offspring.

points.title: Natural selection
points.detail: Variation, selection pressure, differential survival and reproduction, and the increase in the frequency of advantageous alleles over generations.

questions.q: A population of beetles on a dark-soiled island becomes predominantly dark over fifty generations. Explain this change using natural selection.
answer: There was pre-existing variation in colour in the population, caused by different alleles.
Predation acted as a selection pressure, and dark beetles were better camouflaged against the dark soil.
Dark beetles were more likely to survive to reproductive age and pass on their alleles for dark colour.
Over many generations the frequency of the dark allele increased in the population.

points.title: Genetic drift, bottleneck and founder effects
points.detail: Random changes in allele frequency in small populations; the bottleneck effect after a population crash and the founder effect when a small group establishes a new population.

questions.q: Distinguish between the bottleneck effect and the founder effect, and state one consequence common to both.
answer: A bottleneck occurs when a population is drastically reduced by an event such as a disaster, leaving a small unrepresentative group of survivors.
The founder effect occurs when a small group leaves and establishes a new population elsewhere.
Both produce a population with reduced genetic diversity whose allele frequencies differ from the original population by chance, making it more vulnerable to environmental change and disease.

points.title: Gene flow
points.detail: Movement of alleles between populations through migration and interbreeding, and its effect of reducing genetic differences between populations.

questions.q: Explain how gene flow between two populations affects the likelihood that they will become separate species.
answer: Gene flow introduces alleles from one population into the other, making their gene pools more similar.
This counteracts the divergence produced by different selection pressures, mutation and drift.
Speciation is therefore less likely while gene flow continues, and more likely once populations are isolated.

points.title: Antibiotic and pesticide resistance
points.detail: Resistance arising from pre-existing variation, the antibiotic acting as a selection pressure, and the role of overuse and incomplete courses in spreading resistant strains.

questions.q: Explain how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic, and why finishing a full course of antibiotics matters.
answer: Random mutation produces a small number of bacteria that already carry an allele conferring resistance before the antibiotic is used.
The antibiotic acts as a selection pressure and kills the non-resistant bacteria.
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce rapidly, so the frequency of the resistance allele increases in the population.
Stopping a course early leaves partially resistant bacteria alive to reproduce, and resistance genes can also spread horizontally on plasmids.

points.title: Selective breeding
points.detail: Artificial selection of desirable phenotypes over generations, its similarities to and differences from natural selection, and the risk of reduced genetic diversity.

questions.q: Compare artificial selection with natural selection and state one risk of long-term selective breeding.
answer: Both rely on existing variation and both change allele frequencies over generations.
In artificial selection humans choose which individuals breed for a desired trait, whereas in natural selection the environment determines differential survival and reproduction.
Long-term selective breeding narrows the gene pool, leaving the population vulnerable to disease and reducing the variation available for future change.

points.title: Speciation
points.detail: Allopatric speciation following geographic isolation and sympatric speciation without it; the accumulation of differences until reproductive isolation is complete.

questions.q: Describe how allopatric speciation could produce two species of lizard from one original population.
answer: A geographic barrier such as a river or mountain range divides the original population into two, preventing gene flow.
The two populations experience different selection pressures and accumulate different mutations.
Genetic drift and natural selection cause the gene pools to diverge over many generations.
The populations eventually become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, even if they meet again, and are therefore separate species.

points.title: The fossil record
points.detail: Conditions required for fossilisation, types of fossils, index and transitional fossils, and why the fossil record is incomplete.

questions.q: Explain what a transitional fossil shows and why the fossil record is incomplete.
answer: A transitional fossil has features of two groups and provides evidence of a link between an ancestral and a descendant group.
Fossilisation requires rapid burial in the absence of oxygen and decomposers, which occurs rarely.
Soft-bodied organisms fossilise poorly, many fossils are destroyed by geological processes, and only a fraction of those formed have been found.

points.title: Dating techniques
points.detail: Relative dating by stratigraphy and index fossils; absolute dating by radiometric decay and half-life; choosing a technique appropriate to the age of the sample.

questions.q: A fossil is estimated to be about two million years old. Explain why carbon-14 dating would not be suitable and suggest an alternative.
answer: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years, so after two million years almost no carbon-14 remains to measure.
An isotope with a much longer half-life, such as potassium-40, would be used instead.
Potassium-40 dating is applied to volcanic rock layers above and below the fossil to bracket its age.

points.title: Structural morphology as evidence
points.detail: Homologous structures indicating common ancestry through divergent evolution, analogous structures indicating convergent evolution, and vestigial structures.

questions.q: Distinguish between homologous and analogous structures and state what each indicates about relatedness.
answer: Homologous structures have a similar underlying structure but may have different functions, such as the pentadactyl limb of a human, whale and bat.
They indicate descent from a common ancestor followed by divergent evolution.
Analogous structures have similar functions but different underlying structures, such as the wings of an insect and a bird, and indicate convergent evolution rather than close relatedness.

points.title: Molecular homology
points.detail: Comparison of DNA and amino acid sequences between species, and the inference that fewer differences indicate a more recent common ancestor.

questions.q: A protein from species X differs from the human version at 4 amino acids, and from species Y at 27. Interpret this evidence.
answer: Species X shares a more recent common ancestor with humans than species Y does.
Fewer sequence differences indicate that less time has elapsed for mutations to accumulate since the lineages diverged.
Molecular evidence is used alongside structural and fossil evidence because rates of change can vary between proteins and lineages.

points.title: Molecular clocks
points.detail: The assumption of an approximately constant rate of mutation in selectively neutral regions, calibration against the fossil record, and limitations of the method.

questions.q: State the key assumption underlying the molecular clock and one limitation of the technique.
answer: It assumes that mutations accumulate at an approximately constant rate over time in the sequence being compared.
A limitation is that mutation rates differ between genes, species and time periods, particularly where selection is acting.
Clocks must therefore be calibrated against independently dated fossil evidence.

points.title: Phylogenetic trees
points.detail: Reading nodes as common ancestors, branch points as divergence events, and using shared derived characteristics to construct and interpret trees.

questions.q: Explain how to determine from a phylogenetic tree which of two species is more closely related to a third.
answer: Trace back from each species to the node where its lineage meets that of the third species.
The species whose most recent common ancestor with the third species is closer to the tips is the more closely related.
Physical similarity and the order of the branch tips along the page are not reliable guides; only branching order matters.

points.title: Extinction and mass extinction events
points.detail: Causes of extinction, characteristics that make species vulnerable, and how mass extinctions open niches and accelerate diversification of surviving groups.

questions.q: Explain why a specialist species with a small population is more vulnerable to extinction than a generalist with a large range.
answer: A specialist depends on a narrow range of food or habitat, so a change in those conditions removes its resources entirely.
A small population has reduced genetic diversity, so it is less likely to contain alleles that suit the new conditions.
A generalist can switch resources and a large range means local changes affect only part of the population.

points.title: Hominin characteristics and trends
points.detail: Bipedalism and the associated skeletal changes, increasing cranial capacity, reduced prognathism and dentition, and the use of these features to interpret hominin fossils.

questions.q: Identify two skeletal features that indicate a hominin fossil was bipedal and explain how each supports upright walking.
answer: A foramen magnum positioned centrally under the skull balances the head directly above the spine.
A short, broad, bowl-shaped pelvis supports the internal organs and anchors muscles used in upright walking.
An S-shaped spine, angled femur and non-opposable big toe with an arched foot also indicate weight bearing and striding.

points.title: Homo sapiens, Neanderthals and human migration
points.detail: Evidence for the out-of-Africa model, comparisons between Homo sapiens and Homo neanderthalensis, and evidence of interbreeding from Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA.

questions.q: Describe two lines of evidence that support the out-of-Africa model of modern human origins.
answer: The oldest Homo sapiens fossils are found in Africa, with progressively younger fossils found further from Africa.
Genetic diversity is greatest in African populations, consistent with a longer period of accumulated mutation there.
Mitochondrial DNA and Y chromosome lineages of modern populations trace back to African ancestors, while Neanderthal DNA in non-African genomes indicates later interbreeding during migration.

points.title: Designing the investigation
points.detail: Selecting a question within a designated topic, developing an aim and hypothesis, choosing a methodology and planning a repeatable method with appropriate controls.

questions.q: Outline three decisions that must be made when designing a controlled experiment, and explain why each affects the validity of the results.
answer: Choosing which variable to manipulate and which to measure determines whether the investigation actually tests the hypothesis.
Deciding which variables to control prevents extraneous variables from confounding the results.
Choosing the number of trials and the sample size affects how well random error and individual variation are accounted for.

points.title: Logbook, safety and ethics
points.detail: Maintaining a logbook as an authenticated record of planning, changes and raw data; risk assessment; ethical considerations for organisms and participants.

questions.q: Explain why a logbook is required and what should be recorded in it if a method is changed part-way through an investigation.
answer: The logbook is an authenticated primary record that allows the work to be verified and reproduced.
Any change to the method must be recorded with the date and the reason for the change.
Data collected before and after the change must be clearly distinguished so that results are interpreted correctly.

points.title: Generating and recording data
points.detail: Collecting primary quantitative and qualitative data, choosing appropriate units and precision, and organising raw data into tables with headings and units.

questions.q: State two features of a well-constructed results table and explain why each is needed.
answer: Column headings include the quantity and its unit, so readers can interpret the values without ambiguity.
Values are recorded to a consistent number of decimal places reflecting the precision of the instrument.
Raw data and processed values such as means are shown separately so calculations can be checked.

points.title: Analysing and evaluating results
points.detail: Identifying trends and relationships, distinguishing correlation from causation, evaluating the accuracy, precision, repeatability and validity of the method, and suggesting improvements.

questions.q: An investigation produced results that broadly matched the hypothesis but had a large spread between trials. Evaluate this outcome and suggest one improvement.
answer: The large spread indicates low precision, most likely caused by random error in measurement or uncontrolled variation between samples.
The conclusion can still be supported, but with reduced confidence, and the limitation must be stated.
Increasing the number of trials and tightening control of extraneous variables would reduce the spread.

points.title: Communicating with a scientific poster
points.detail: The structure of a scientific poster including title, introduction, methodology and method, results, discussion and conclusion, and conventions for referencing and figures.

questions.q: State what belongs in the discussion section of a scientific poster, and how it differs from the conclusion.
answer: The discussion interprets the results, links them to the hypothesis and relevant biology, and evaluates limitations and sources of error.
The conclusion is a brief statement of what was found in relation to the aim, without new interpretation.
The discussion may also suggest further investigations; the conclusion should not introduce information not supported by the results.

name: Chemistry
areas: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
Unit 4 — Structure and naming of organic compounds
source: Adapted revision checklist based on VCAA's VCE Chemistry Study Design, Units 3 and 4. Areas here are topic groupings rather than official area of study titles, and checklist numbers are internal tracker IDs.
practiceNote: These practice questions and marking guides are original revision exercises, not VCAA examination questions. Use class resources, the data book and past examinations for official practice.
papers: Use the VCAA examination specifications, past examinations and examination reports for official assessment resources.

points.title: Aims, hypotheses and variables
points.detail: Writing a research question and a testable hypothesis; identifying the independent, dependent and controlled variables in a chemical investigation.

questions.q: A student investigates how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of reaction with magnesium ribbon. Write a hypothesis and identify all three variable types.
answer: Hypothesis: as the concentration of hydrochloric acid increases, the rate of reaction with magnesium will increase.
Independent variable: concentration of hydrochloric acid.
Dependent variable: rate of reaction, for example volume of hydrogen collected per unit time.
Controlled variables include temperature, surface area and mass of magnesium, and volume of acid.

points.title: Accuracy, precision and validity
points.detail: Distinguishing accuracy from precision; repeatability and reproducibility; validity of a method and of a conclusion; the role of a standard or known sample.

questions.q: Three titrations give concordant titres that are all 0.40 mL higher than the true value. Describe the accuracy and precision and identify the likely cause.
answer: The results are precise because the titres agree closely with one another.
They are not accurate because all results are displaced from the true value in the same direction.
This pattern indicates a systematic error, such as a burette that was not rinsed with the titrant or an incorrectly standardised solution.

points.title: Uncertainty, significant figures and errors
points.detail: Recording measurements to the precision of the instrument, propagating uncertainty through calculations, expressing answers to an appropriate number of significant figures, and classifying random, systematic and personal errors.

questions.q: A mass of 2.50 g is dissolved in 250.0 mL of solution. State how many significant figures the calculated concentration should be reported to and justify your answer.
answer: The answer should be reported to three significant figures.
In multiplication and division the result carries the same number of significant figures as the least precise measurement.
The mass 2.50 g has three significant figures, which is fewer than the four in 250.0 mL.

points.title: Using the data book and chemical conventions
points.detail: Locating standard electrode potentials, molar masses, enthalpy data and spectroscopic tables; using correct state symbols, formulae and units throughout working.

questions.q: State two conventions that must be followed when writing a thermochemical equation, and explain why each matters.
answer: State symbols must be included, because the enthalpy change depends on whether reactants and products are solid, liquid, gas or aqueous.
The enthalpy change must be quoted with a sign and with units of kJ per mole for the equation as written.
Doubling the coefficients doubles the enthalpy change, so the equation and the value must match.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Renewable and non-renewable fuels
points.detail: Classifying fossil fuels, biofuels and other energy sources as renewable or non-renewable; comparing them on availability, greenhouse emissions and energy density.

questions.q: Compare biodiesel with petrodiesel in terms of renewability and net carbon dioxide emissions.
answer: Biodiesel is renewable because it is produced from plant or animal oils that can be regrown within a human timescale.
Petrodiesel is non-renewable because crude oil formed over millions of years and is consumed far faster than it forms.
Biodiesel has a lower net carbon dioxide output because the crops absorb carbon dioxide during growth, although production and transport still release some.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Complete and incomplete combustion
points.detail: Writing balanced equations for complete and incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons and alcohols; the products formed and the consequences of incomplete combustion.

questions.q: Write a balanced equation for the incomplete combustion of octane producing carbon monoxide only, and state one hazard of incomplete combustion.
answer: 2 C8H18(l) + 17 O2(g) produces 16 CO(g) + 18 H2O(g).
Incomplete combustion releases less energy per mole of fuel than complete combustion.
Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds irreversibly to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport, and soot particulates cause respiratory harm.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Thermochemical equations and enthalpy
points.detail: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, the sign convention for enthalpy change, and scaling enthalpy with the coefficients of the equation.

questions.q: The combustion of one mole of methane releases 890 kJ. Write the thermochemical equation and state the enthalpy change when 0.25 mol is burned.
answer: CH4(g) + 2 O2(g) produces CO2(g) + 2 H2O(l), with an enthalpy change of negative 890 kJ per mole.
Burning 0.25 mol releases 0.25 multiplied by 890, which is 222.5 kJ.
The enthalpy change is negative 222.5 kJ because the reaction is exothermic.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Energy profile diagrams and catalysts
points.detail: Labelling reactants, products, activation energy, the activated complex and the enthalpy change; the effect of a catalyst on the activation energy but not the enthalpy change.

questions.q: Sketch in words how an energy profile diagram changes when a catalyst is added to an exothermic reaction, and explain the effect on the enthalpy change.
answer: A second, lower curve appears with a smaller activation energy hump, representing the alternative reaction pathway.
The energy levels of the reactants and products are unchanged.
The enthalpy change is therefore unchanged, because it depends only on the difference between reactant and product energies.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Energy density and calculations
points.detail: Calculating the energy released per gram or per litre of a fuel, and comparing fuels on both an energy density and a mass or volume basis.

questions.q: Ethanol releases 1364 kJ per mole on complete combustion. Calculate its energy density in kJ per gram and comment on how it compares with octane at about 48 kJ per gram.
answer: The molar mass of ethanol, C2H5OH, is 46.0 g per mole.
Energy density is 1364 divided by 46.0, which is 29.7 kJ per gram.
Ethanol has a lower energy density than octane because the carbon in ethanol is already partly oxidised, so less energy is released per gram.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Calorimetry and calibration
points.detail: Solution calorimetry and bomb calorimetry, the calibration factor determined electrically or from a known reaction, and the calculation of energy released by a sample.

questions.q: Explain why a bomb calorimeter is calibrated before use and describe how a calibration factor is determined electrically.
answer: Calibration determines how much energy is required to raise the calorimeter temperature by one degree Celsius, since heat is absorbed by the whole apparatus, not just the water.
A known electrical energy is supplied by passing a measured current at a measured voltage for a measured time, and the temperature rise is recorded.
The calibration factor is the electrical energy supplied divided by the temperature change, in joules per degree Celsius.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Sources of error in calorimetry
points.detail: Heat loss to the surroundings, incomplete combustion, evaporation and the effect of each on the calculated enthalpy change; improvements to reduce error.

questions.q: A solution calorimetry experiment gives an enthalpy of combustion lower in magnitude than the accepted value. Give two reasons and classify the type of error.
answer: Heat is lost to the surroundings rather than being transferred to the water, so the measured temperature rise is too small.
Incomplete combustion means less energy is released per mole of fuel burned.
Both are systematic errors, because they shift every result in the same direction; insulating the apparatus and ensuring adequate oxygen would reduce them.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Oxidation numbers and redox
points.detail: Assigning oxidation numbers, identifying the species oxidised and reduced, and naming the oxidising and reducing agents in a redox reaction.

questions.q: In the reaction between zinc metal and copper(II) ions, identify what is oxidised, what is reduced and name the oxidising agent.
answer: Zinc is oxidised, as its oxidation number rises from 0 to positive 2 and it loses two electrons.
Copper(II) ions are reduced, as the oxidation number falls from positive 2 to 0.
The copper(II) ion is the oxidising agent because it accepts electrons and is itself reduced.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Writing and balancing half-equations
points.detail: Balancing half-equations in acidic conditions using water, hydrogen ions and electrons, and combining half-equations so that electrons cancel.

questions.q: Balance the half-equation for the reduction of the permanganate ion to the manganese(II) ion in acidic solution.
answer: Balance manganese first: MnO4 minus becomes Mn 2 plus.
Balance oxygen with water and hydrogen with hydrogen ions: MnO4 minus plus 8 H plus gives Mn 2 plus plus 4 H2O.
Balance charge with electrons: MnO4 minus plus 8 H plus plus 5 electrons gives Mn 2 plus plus 4 H2O.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Galvanic cell structure and operation
points.detail: Anode, cathode, electrolytes, salt bridge and external circuit; the direction of electron and ion flow; polarity of each electrode.

questions.q: Describe the role of the salt bridge in a galvanic cell and state the direction in which each type of ion moves.
answer: The salt bridge completes the circuit by allowing ions to move between the two half-cells.
It maintains electrical neutrality, because the anode half-cell accumulates positive charge and the cathode half-cell accumulates negative charge.
Anions move through the bridge towards the anode half-cell, and cations move towards the cathode half-cell.
Without it, charge build-up would stop electron flow almost immediately.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: The electrochemical series and cell voltage
points.detail: Using standard electrode potentials to predict the spontaneous direction of a redox reaction and to calculate the maximum cell voltage under standard conditions.

questions.q: Using standard electrode potentials, explain how to determine which half-cell is the anode and calculate the cell voltage.
answer: The half-cell with the more negative standard electrode potential undergoes oxidation and is the anode.
The half-cell with the more positive potential undergoes reduction and is the cathode.
The cell voltage is the reduction potential of the cathode minus the reduction potential of the anode, and a positive value indicates a spontaneous reaction.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Limitations of the electrochemical series
points.detail: Why predictions may fail: non-standard concentrations and temperature, the state of the electrode surface, competing reactions and reaction rate.

questions.q: A predicted spontaneous reaction does not occur at a measurable rate. Explain why the electrochemical series may fail to predict what happens in practice.
answer: The electrochemical series predicts whether a reaction is thermodynamically favourable, not how fast it occurs.
The values apply only at standard conditions of 1 molar solutions, 100 kPa and 25 degrees Celsius; different conditions change the potentials.
Surface coatings, passivation or the presence of alternative reactions such as water being oxidised may also alter the outcome.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Primary, secondary and fuel cells
points.detail: Comparing single-use, rechargeable and continuously fed cells on reversibility, lifetime and application; the structure of a hydrogen fuel cell.

questions.q: Distinguish between a primary cell, a secondary cell and a fuel cell.
answer: A primary cell is not rechargeable, because the products are unable to be converted back to reactants by applying a voltage.
A secondary cell is rechargeable, as the electrode reactions can be reversed by an applied external voltage.
A fuel cell is continuously supplied with reactants from an external source, so it does not run down provided the fuel supply continues.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Hydrogen fuel cells
points.detail: Half-equations in acidic and alkaline electrolytes, the overall reaction, and the advantages and disadvantages compared with combustion of fossil fuels.

questions.q: Write the half-equations and overall equation for an acidic hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, and state one advantage over a petrol engine.
answer: Anode: H2(g) gives 2 H plus plus 2 electrons.
Cathode: O2(g) plus 4 H plus plus 4 electrons gives 2 H2O(l).
Overall: 2 H2(g) plus O2(g) gives 2 H2O(l).
An advantage is higher energy efficiency, because chemical energy is converted directly to electrical energy without the thermal losses of a heat engine, and the only product is water.

points.area: Unit 3 — Energy, fuels and galvanic cells
points.title: Faraday's laws and electrochemical calculations
points.detail: Using charge equals current multiplied by time, the Faraday constant and the mole ratio in a half-equation to calculate the mass of product or the time required.

questions.q: A current of 2.00 A is passed for 30.0 minutes through a cell depositing copper from copper(II) ions. Calculate the mass of copper deposited.
answer: Charge equals 2.00 multiplied by 1800 seconds, which is 3600 C.
Moles of electrons equals 3600 divided by 96500, which is 0.0373 mol; the half-equation requires 2 electrons per copper, so moles of copper is 0.01865 mol.
Mass equals 0.01865 multiplied by 63.5, which is 1.18 g.

points.title: Collision theory and rate
points.detail: Successful collisions requiring sufficient energy and correct orientation; the relationship between the frequency of successful collisions and reaction rate.

questions.q: Using collision theory, explain why not every collision between reactant particles results in a reaction.
answer: Particles must collide with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy to break the existing bonds.
Particles must also collide with the correct orientation so that the reacting parts of the molecules meet.
Collisions failing either condition are unsuccessful and the particles simply rebound.

points.title: Factors affecting reaction rate
points.detail: Temperature, concentration, pressure, surface area and catalysts explained in terms of collision frequency and the proportion of particles with sufficient energy.

questions.q: Explain in terms of collision theory why a small increase in temperature can produce a large increase in reaction rate.
answer: Increasing temperature increases the average kinetic energy, so particles move faster and collide more frequently.
More importantly, a much greater proportion of particles now has energy exceeding the activation energy.
The number of successful collisions per second therefore rises sharply, which has a larger effect than collision frequency alone.

points.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions
points.detail: Interpreting the distribution of particle energies, the shift with temperature, and the shaded region beyond the activation energy with and without a catalyst.

questions.q: Describe how a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve changes when the temperature is raised, and what this shows about reaction rate.
answer: The peak of the curve becomes lower and shifts to the right, towards higher energies.
The total area under the curve is unchanged because the number of particles is unchanged.
A larger area lies beyond the activation energy, showing that a greater proportion of particles can react, so the rate increases.

points.title: Catalysts and reaction pathways
points.detail: How a catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, the difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts, and why a catalyst is not consumed.

questions.q: Explain why adding a catalyst increases the rate of both the forward and the reverse reaction equally, and state the effect on the equilibrium position.
answer: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, because it provides one alternative pathway.
Both rates therefore increase by the same factor.
Equilibrium is reached sooner but the equilibrium position and the value of the equilibrium constant are unchanged.

points.title: Dynamic equilibrium
points.detail: The characteristics of dynamic equilibrium in a closed system: equal forward and reverse rates, constant macroscopic properties and continuing molecular change.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by dynamic equilibrium and state two observations consistent with a system being at equilibrium.
answer: Dynamic equilibrium occurs in a closed system when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
Reactions continue at the molecular level, but the concentrations of all species remain constant.
Observations include a constant colour intensity and a constant pressure or concentration over time.

points.title: The equilibrium constant
points.detail: Writing an expression for the equilibrium constant, the effect of changing the equation, units, and what the magnitude of the constant indicates about the extent of reaction.

questions.q: For a reaction, K equals 1.0 times 10 to the power of negative 5 at 500 K. State what this indicates and how K changes if the equation is reversed.
answer: A very small K indicates that at equilibrium the mixture consists mainly of reactants, so the reaction proceeds only to a small extent.
Reversing the equation gives an equilibrium constant equal to the reciprocal, which is 1.0 times 10 to the power of 5.
K changes only with temperature, not with concentration, pressure or the presence of a catalyst.

points.title: Le Chatelier's principle
points.detail: Predicting the effect of changes in concentration, pressure, volume and temperature on the equilibrium position, and explaining the direction of the net change.

questions.q: For an exothermic gaseous reaction with fewer moles of gas on the product side, predict and explain the effect of increasing the temperature.
answer: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, which here is the reverse reaction.
The equilibrium position shifts to the left, so the yield of product decreases.
The equilibrium constant also decreases, because K changes with temperature.

points.title: Concentration-time and rate graphs
points.detail: Interpreting the shape of concentration-time graphs after a disturbance, including the instantaneous jump for a concentration change and the gradual change for temperature.

questions.q: Describe how the concentration-time graph differs when equilibrium is disturbed by adding more reactant compared with raising the temperature.
answer: Adding reactant produces an immediate vertical jump in that species only, followed by a gradual curve as the system re-establishes equilibrium.
Raising the temperature produces no instantaneous jump; all concentrations change gradually as both rates increase.
A temperature change also alters the value of K, whereas a concentration change does not.
