questions.q: Define the terms of trade and explain the effects of a sustained improvement on the Australian economy.
answer: The terms of trade is the ratio of the index of export prices to the index of import prices, expressed as an index.
An improvement means export prices have risen relative to import prices, so a given volume of exports buys more imports.
Export revenue and national income rise, boosting incomes in the export sector, company profits and tax receipts, which supports growth and the budget position.
An improvement usually also causes the dollar to appreciate, which reduces the competitiveness of other export and import-competing industries.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 3 — Australia and the international economy
points.title: The balance of payments
points.detail: The structure of the current account and the capital and financial account, the meaning of a deficit or surplus, and the relationship between the two accounts.

questions.q: Describe the two main accounts in the balance of payments and explain what each records.
answer: The current account records the net value of transactions in goods and services, primary income and secondary income.
The balance on goods and services is the difference between export and import receipts; the net primary income balance records interest and dividends paid to and received from overseas.
The capital and financial account records transactions in assets, including foreign investment into and out of Australia.
In principle a deficit on the current account is offset by a surplus on the capital and financial account, since the two must sum to zero.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 3 — Australia and the international economy
points.title: Free trade agreements
points.detail: Bilateral and multilateral agreements, the trade creation and trade diversion effects, and the impact on Australian industries and living standards.

questions.q: Explain one benefit and one cost of Australia entering a bilateral free trade agreement.
answer: A benefit is improved access to a large overseas market for Australian exporters, raising export revenue, employment and incomes in those industries.
Consumers also gain from cheaper imports from the partner country.
A cost is trade diversion, where trade shifts to the partner country even though a third country is a lower-cost producer, which is allocatively inefficient.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 3 — Australia and the international economy
points.title: Foreign investment
points.detail: Foreign direct and portfolio investment, the reasons for investment inflows, and the effects on capacity, growth and the current account.

questions.q: Explain one benefit and one cost of foreign direct investment in Australia.
answer: A benefit is that foreign investment supplements domestic saving and funds capital projects that would otherwise not proceed.
This expands productive capacity, raises productivity through access to new technology and management practice, and creates employment.
A cost is that returns on that investment flow overseas as dividends and interest, adding to the net primary income outflow and widening the current account deficit.
There may also be concerns about foreign control of strategic assets and reduced domestic decision-making power.

points.title: Sources of budget revenue
points.detail: Direct taxes including personal income tax and company tax, indirect taxes including GST and excise, and non-tax revenue.

questions.q: Distinguish between direct and indirect taxes and explain why personal income tax is progressive.
answer: A direct tax is levied on the income or wealth of the individual or entity that bears it, such as personal income tax and company tax.
An indirect tax is levied on a transaction and can be passed on to another party, such as the GST and excise duties.
Personal income tax is progressive because the marginal rate rises as income rises, so higher income earners pay a larger proportion of their income in tax.
This reduces inequality in the distribution of income and improves equity.

points.title: Budget expenses
points.detail: Government current spending on goods and services, capital spending on infrastructure, and transfer payments, and the different effects of each on aggregate demand.

questions.q: Distinguish between government current spending, capital spending and transfer payments, and state which has the largest immediate effect on aggregate demand.
answer: Current spending is on day-to-day goods and services such as public sector wages; capital spending is on infrastructure such as roads and hospitals.
Transfer payments, such as pensions and unemployment benefits, redistribute income without the government receiving a good or service in return.
Government spending on goods and services has a direct and immediate effect on aggregate demand, whereas transfers affect demand only once recipients spend them, and some is saved.

points.title: Budget outcomes and financing
points.detail: Surplus, deficit and balanced outcomes, the difference between cash and underlying outcomes, and how a deficit is financed and a surplus used.

questions.q: Explain what a budget deficit is and describe two ways it may be financed, including the effect of each.
answer: A budget deficit occurs when total budget expenses exceed total budget receipts in a financial year.
It may be financed by borrowing from the private sector through the issue of government bonds, which adds to public debt and interest obligations.
Heavy domestic borrowing may crowd out private investment by placing upward pressure on interest rates.
It may also be financed by borrowing from overseas, which avoids crowding out domestically but adds to the net primary income outflow on the current account.

points.title: Automatic and discretionary stabilisers
points.detail: The countercyclical operation of progressive income tax and unemployment benefits, and the distinction from deliberate discretionary policy changes.

questions.q: Explain how automatic stabilisers operate during a downturn and how they differ from discretionary policy.
answer: During a downturn incomes fall, so progressive income tax receipts fall more than proportionately, leaving households with more disposable income than they would otherwise have.
Unemployment benefits rise automatically as more people lose work, supporting their spending.
Both effects expand the budget deficit and cushion the fall in aggregate demand without any government decision being required.
Discretionary policy is a deliberate change to tax rates or spending programs announced by the government, which takes longer to implement but can be targeted.

points.title: Budgetary policy stance
points.detail: Expansionary and contractionary stances judged by the change in the budget outcome rather than by whether it is in deficit or surplus.

questions.q: A budget moves from a deficit of 40 billion to a deficit of 15 billion. Identify the stance and explain your reasoning.
answer: The stance is contractionary, because the deficit has narrowed by 25 billion.
Stance is determined by the change in the budget outcome from one year to the next, not by whether the budget is in deficit or surplus.
A smaller deficit means the budget is injecting less into the economy than previously, so aggregate demand is being dampened relative to the prior year.

points.title: Strengths and weaknesses of budgetary policy
points.detail: The ability to target specific sectors, the effects on equity and supply capacity, against implementation lags, political constraints and debt accumulation.

questions.q: Evaluate budgetary policy by explaining one strength and one weakness as a demand management tool.
answer: A strength is that budgetary policy can be targeted at a specific group, region or industry, such as a payment to low income households who are likely to spend it.
It can also address equity directly through the tax and transfer system, which monetary policy cannot do.
A weakness is the implementation lag, since major changes are usually announced in the annual budget and take time to legislate and take effect.
Political constraints also apply, as governments are reluctant to raise taxes or cut spending, which can make contractionary policy difficult to sustain.

points.title: Monetary policy and the cash rate
points.detail: The role of the Reserve Bank of Australia, the setting of the cash rate target, and its independence from government.

questions.q: Explain what the cash rate is and why the RBA's independence from government matters.
answer: The cash rate is the interest rate on overnight loans between financial institutions in the cash market, and the RBA sets a target for it.
Changes in the cash rate flow through to the interest rates banks charge borrowers and pay savers.
Independence matters because the RBA can raise rates to control inflation without the political pressure that would deter an elected government, which makes the inflation target credible.

points.title: Transmission mechanisms of monetary policy
points.detail: The savings and investment, cash flow, asset prices and exchange rate channels through which a change in the cash rate affects aggregate demand.

questions.q: Explain three channels through which a cut in the cash rate stimulates aggregate demand.
answer: Cash flow channel: households with variable rate mortgages have lower repayments, leaving more disposable income for consumption.
Savings and investment channel: the return on saving falls and the cost of borrowing falls, encouraging consumption and making more investment projects profitable.
Asset prices channel: lower rates raise share and property prices, and the resulting wealth effect encourages households to spend more.
Exchange rate channel: lower relative interest rates reduce demand for the dollar, causing a depreciation that raises net exports.

points.title: Monetary policy stance
points.detail: Expansionary, contractionary and neutral stances, the concept of the neutral cash rate, and the reading of a stance from RBA decisions.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by a neutral monetary policy stance.
answer: A neutral stance is one in which the cash rate is at the level that neither stimulates nor dampens aggregate demand.
At this rate, growth is expected to proceed at a sustainable pace with inflation within the target band.
A rate below neutral is expansionary and a rate above neutral is contractionary, so the stance is judged relative to the neutral rate rather than by the level of the rate alone.

points.title: Strengths and weaknesses of monetary policy
points.detail: Independence, speed of decision and flexibility against blunt sector-wide impact, transmission lags and reduced effectiveness at very low interest rates.

questions.q: Evaluate monetary policy by explaining one strength and two weaknesses.
answer: A strength is that the RBA board meets regularly and can change the cash rate quickly and independently of political considerations, with immediate effect on market rates.
A weakness is that monetary policy is a blunt instrument affecting the whole economy, so it cannot target a particular region or sector in difficulty.
There is also an impact lag of up to 18 months before a change in the cash rate fully affects spending and inflation.
At very low interest rates its effectiveness is reduced, since rates cannot fall much further and confidence rather than the cost of borrowing may be the constraint on spending.

points.title: Policy mix and complementary policy
points.detail: How budgetary and monetary policy work together or against each other, and the circumstances in which one is better suited than the other.

questions.q: Explain why budgetary policy may be preferred to monetary policy during a severe downturn.
answer: In a severe downturn confidence is low, so households and firms may not borrow and spend even when interest rates are very low.
Interest rates may also already be near zero, leaving little room for further stimulus.
Budgetary policy can inject spending directly into the economy through government spending and transfers, which does not rely on private willingness to borrow.
It can also be targeted at the households and industries most affected, making the stimulus more effective per dollar spent.

points.title: Injections, leakages and the circular flow
points.detail: The circular flow of income, the injections of investment, government spending and exports, the leakages of saving, taxation and imports, and the effect of an imbalance.

questions.q: Name the injections and leakages in the circular flow and explain what happens when injections exceed leakages.
answer: Injections are investment, government spending and exports; leakages are saving, taxation and imports.
When injections exceed leakages, more is being added to the flow of income than is being withdrawn.
Aggregate demand rises, so firms increase output and employment and national income expands.
If this continues beyond the economy's productive capacity it generates demand inflation, so the imbalance is sustainable only while spare capacity exists.

points.title: Public debt and crowding out
points.detail: The accumulation of government debt from sustained deficits, the interest burden on future budgets, and the crowding out of private sector investment.

questions.q: Explain the crowding out effect and one further consequence of sustained budget deficits.
answer: Financing a deficit by borrowing from the domestic private sector increases the demand for available funds.
This places upward pressure on interest rates, raising the cost of borrowing for households and businesses.
Some private investment projects become unprofitable and do not proceed, so public spending has partly displaced private spending.
Sustained deficits also accumulate public debt, and the growing interest bill consumes budget revenue that could otherwise fund services or tax cuts.

points.title: The purpose of aggregate supply policies
points.detail: Expanding productive capacity, lowering the costs of production and raising productivity so that growth can occur without inflation.

questions.q: Explain how aggregate supply policies help resolve the trade-off between the goals of low inflation and full employment.
answer: Aggregate supply policies raise productive capacity and lower unit costs of production, shifting aggregate supply to the right.
The economy can then produce more output without the capacity constraints that generate demand inflation.
Lower unit costs also reduce cost inflationary pressure even as employment rises.
This allows both stronger growth and employment and lower inflation at the same time, easing the short-run trade-off.

points.title: Budgetary supply-side measures
points.detail: Spending on education, training, infrastructure and research, and tax measures such as investment incentives that expand capacity rather than demand.

questions.q: Explain how government spending on infrastructure acts as both an aggregate demand and an aggregate supply policy.
answer: In the short term, construction spending is an injection into the economy that directly raises aggregate demand and employment.
In the longer term, better transport and communications infrastructure reduces the time and cost of moving goods and people.
Lower costs of production raise productivity and shift aggregate supply to the right.
The policy therefore stimulates demand now and expands capacity later, which is why infrastructure is often used during downturns.

points.title: Training, education and skilled migration
points.detail: Policies that increase the quantity and quality of labour, address skill shortages and raise participation.

questions.q: Explain how a targeted skilled migration program acts as an aggregate supply policy.
answer: Skilled migration increases the size and skill level of the labour force, addressing shortages in specific occupations.
Relieving skill shortages reduces upward pressure on wages in those occupations, lowering the cost of production.
Productive capacity expands and aggregate supply shifts to the right, supporting growth with less inflationary pressure.

points.title: Trade liberalisation and competition policy
points.detail: Removing protection and promoting competition to force efficiency improvements, and the structural adjustment costs involved.

questions.q: Explain how competition policy improves efficiency and one cost of relying on it.
answer: Competition policy prevents anti-competitive conduct and reduces barriers to entry so that firms face genuine rivals.
Firms must reduce costs and innovate to retain market share, improving productive and dynamic efficiency.
Lower unit costs shift aggregate supply to the right and prices to consumers fall, improving material living standards.
A cost is structural adjustment, as less efficient firms exit and their workers face unemployment until they retrain and relocate.

points.title: Labour market and deregulation policies
points.detail: Measures affecting wage determination, workplace flexibility and industry regulation, and their effects on costs, productivity and equity.

questions.q: Explain how labour market policies can improve aggregate supply and one equity concern they raise.
answer: Policies that allow wages to be linked to productivity at the enterprise level mean wage growth does not outpace output growth, containing unit labour costs.
Greater flexibility in working arrangements can raise participation and allow firms to match labour to demand, improving productivity.
Aggregate supply shifts right, supporting growth with lower inflationary pressure.
An equity concern is that increased flexibility may reduce job security and bargaining power for low-skilled workers, widening income inequality.

points.title: Environmental and energy policies
points.detail: Policies addressing emissions and energy costs, and the tension between short-run costs of production and long-run intertemporal efficiency.

questions.q: Explain the short-run and long-run effects of a policy subsidising renewable energy investment on aggregate supply.
answer: In the short run the subsidy is a budget cost, and the transition may raise energy costs for some producers, restraining aggregate supply.
In the long run, cheaper and more reliable energy lowers a significant input cost across the economy.
This raises productivity and shifts aggregate supply to the right, supporting non-inflationary growth.
It also improves intertemporal efficiency by reducing the environmental costs imposed on future generations, supporting non-material living standards.

points.title: Evaluating supply-side policies
points.detail: The long implementation and impact lags, budgetary costs and distributional effects of supply-side measures, compared with demand-side policy.

questions.q: Explain two limitations of relying on aggregate supply policies to manage the economy.
answer: Supply-side policies have very long impact lags; education and infrastructure investment may take a decade to raise productive capacity measurably.
They are therefore poorly suited to stabilising the economy over the business cycle, where a rapid response is needed.
Many involve substantial budgetary cost, which worsens the budget outcome and adds to public debt in the short term.
Some, such as deregulation, produce structural unemployment and widen inequality, so they carry political and equity costs.

points.title: Equity and the distribution of income
points.detail: The distinction between efficiency and equity, the effect of the tax and transfer system on the distribution of income, and the trade-offs policy makers face.

questions.q: Explain the potential trade-off between efficiency and equity using an example from tax policy.
answer: Efficiency concerns the allocation and productive use of resources, while equity concerns the fairness of the distribution of income.
A highly progressive income tax improves equity by redistributing income from higher to lower income earners.
However, high marginal rates may reduce the incentive to work additional hours, invest or take entrepreneurial risk, which reduces efficiency and productive capacity.
Policy makers must therefore balance the equity gains from redistribution against the efficiency cost of reduced incentives.

points.title: Interpreting economic data
points.detail: Reading tables and graphs of GDP growth, inflation, unemployment and the exchange rate, describing trends accurately and quoting figures with units and periods.

questions.q: State three features of a strong description of a trend in economic data.
answer: State the direction of the change and whether it accelerated, slowed or reversed over the period.
Quote specific figures with their units and the periods to which they relate, including the start and end values.
Identify any turning point or anomaly rather than describing only the overall movement.

points.title: Building an economic chain of reasoning
points.detail: Linking a cause to an effect through each intermediate step, and connecting the final step back to a macroeconomic goal or to living standards.

questions.q: Explain what a complete chain of reasoning looks like in an Economics response and why missing links cost marks.
answer: Begin with the cause, then state each step in sequence: the effect on a component of aggregate demand or supply, then on the relevant economic variable.
Then state the effect on the macroeconomic goal, and finally on material or non-material living standards.
Marks are awarded for the links, not just the conclusion, so skipping from cause straight to outcome loses the intermediate marks.
Each step should state the direction of change and the mechanism that produces it.

points.title: Command terms and mark allocation
points.detail: The depth required by identify, describe, explain, analyse, discuss and evaluate, and matching the number of distinct points to the marks available.

questions.q: Explain how the mark allocation should guide the structure of an Economics response.
answer: The number of marks indicates roughly how many distinct linked points are required, so a four-mark explanation needs about four developed links.
Command terms determine the depth: describe requires an account, explain requires reasons and mechanism, and evaluate requires both sides plus a judgement.
Check whether the question asks about one effect or two, and whether it specifies a particular goal or policy, and address exactly what is asked.
